We conduct our major analyses on OpenAlex29—a scientific research database built on the foundation of the Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG)52,53. Supported by non-profit organizations, OpenAlex is continuously updated, providing a sus- tainable global resource for research information. As of March 2025, OpenAlex contains 265.7 million research papers, along with related data about citation, author, institution and so on. Among the mas- sive quantity of papers in the OpenAlex dataset, we select 66,117,158 English research papers published in journals and conferences span- ning from 1980 to 2025 and filter out those with incomplete titles or abstracts. We identify the scientific discipline each paper belongs to by making use of the topics noted in OpenAlex, which are extracted using a natural language processing approach that annotates titles and abstracts with Wikipedia article titles as topics sharing textual similarity. In the raw dataset, these topics form a hierarchical struc- ture and each paper is associated with several. Adopting the 19 basic scientific disciplines in MAG52,53, that is, art, biology, business, chem- istry, computer science, economics, engineering, environmental sci- ence, geography, geology, history, materials science, mathematics, medicine, philosophy, physics, political science, psychology, and sociology, we trace along the hierarchy and determine to which dis- ciplines each topic belongs. We note that because the original topics of one paper may be retraced to different topics, the scientific dis- cipline of each paper may not be unique. In other words, one paper may span two or more academic disciplines, for example, chemistry and biology, which reflects the common phenomena of borderline or interdisciplinary research54. Here we emphasize the adoption of AI methods in conventional natural science disciplines and exclude research developing AI meth- odologies themselves, separating the influence of AI on science from AI’s own invention and refinement. We therefore select biology, medi- cine, chemistry, physics, materials science and geology as represent- atives of natural science disciplines, but exclude computer science and mathematics, where most works introducing and developing AI methods are published. We also exclude art, business, economics, history, philosophy, political science, psychology and sociology to focus on how AI is changing the natural sciences and career trajecto- ries in those sciences. Our six natural science disciplines include the majority of OpenAlex articles, resulting in 41,298,433 papers, con- taining 18,392,040 in biology, 4,209,771 in chemistry and 2,380,666 in geology, 4,755,717 in materials science, 24,315,342 in medicine and 5,138,488 in physics. The selected disciplines cover various dimensions of natural science, representing a broad view of scientific research as a whole. Divide into three stages of AI development We divide the history of AI development into three key eras: the tradi- tional machine learning era (1980–2014), the deep learning era (2015– 2022) and the generative AI era (2023 to present). We consider 1980 as the start of the traditional machine learning era because several land- mark works were published in the 1980s, such as the back-propagating method55,56. We regard the deep learning era to have begun in 2015, as indicated by breakthroughs such as ResNet, which enabled the training of ultra-deep neural networks, revolutionizing fields such as computer vision and speech recognition57. Finally, we define the generative AI era as beginning in 2023, following the publication of ChatGPT—the first widely used large language model—in December 2022. This marked the advent of large-scale transformer-based models capable of strong generalized performance across a wide range of tasks, sparking new applications in natural language processing and beyond. Each of these transitions was driven by advances in algorithms, computational power and data availability, substantially expanding the capabilities and scope of AI for science. Design and fine-tune the language model for AI paper identification Insofar as both a paper’s title and abstract contain important informa- tion about its content, we independently train two separate models on the basis of paper titles and abstracts, and then integrate the two mod- els into an ensembled one by averaging their outputs. The structure of our natural language processing model for paper identification consists of two parts. The backbone network is a twelve-layer BERT model with twelve attention heads in each layer, and the sequence classification head is a linear layer with a two-dimensional output atop the BERT out- put. We normalize the two-dimensional output with a softmax function and obtain the probability that the paper involves AI-assistance. We use the BERT model called BERT-base-uncased from Hugging Face58, which is pre-trained with a large-scale general corpus, and set the maximum length of tokenization to be 16 for titles and 256 for abstracts. We design a two-stage fine-tuning process with training and validation sets, which we extracted from the OpenAlex dataset, to transfer the pre-trained model to our paper identification task. The construction of positive and negative data is different between the two stages. In both stages, we randomly split the positive and negative data into 90% and 10% sets, which correspond to training and validation sets, respectively. We use the training set for model training and use the validation set to select the optimal model. As the numbers of positive and negative cases are unbalanced, we use the bootstrap sample technique on positive cases to balance its number with negative cases at both stages. In the first stage, we construct relatively coarse positive data, only considering eight typical AI journals and conferences, including Nature Machine Intelligence, Machine Learning, Artificial Intelligence, Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR), International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), International Conference on Learning Repre- sentations (ICLR) and the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence and International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI). Among the papers belonging to our chosen six disciplines, we extract all papers published in these venues as positive cases and randomly sample 1% of the remaining papers in our six chosen natural science fields as nega- tive cases, resulting in 26,165 positive and 291,035 negative cases. We fine-tune the pre-trained model for 30 epochs on the training set and select the optimal model according to the F1-score on the validation set. In the second stage, we construct more precise positive data on the basis of the optimal model obtained in the first stage. We identify papers in the whole OpenAlex dataset and aggregate the results for each venue, obtaining the probability that each venue in OpenAlex is an AI venue by averaging the AI probability for all papers within it. We then select the venues with >80% AI probability and >100 papers as AI venues. We also incorporate venues with ‘machine learning’ or ‘artificial intelligence’ in their names. In papers belonging to our six chosen disciplines, we extract all papers published in the selected AI venues as positive cases and randomly sample 1% of those remaining as negative cases, result- ing in 31,311 positive and 231,258 negative cases. We then fine-tune the obtained optimal model in the first stage for another 30 epochs with the new training set and select the best model according to F1-score on the new validation set. Finally, we use optimal ensemble models during both stages to identify all papers that use AI to support natural science research from the selected representative natural science disciplines. Scrutinization of our identification results by disciplinary experts We arbitrarily sample 220 papers (110 papers × 2 groups) from each of the six disciplines, resulting in twelve paper groups in total. We enlisted twelve experts with abundant AI research experience (Sup- plementary Table 1) and assigned three different groups of papers to each. Without revealing the classification results obtained from the BERT model, we queried our experts on whether each paper was an AI paper. In this way, each paper is repeatedly labelled by three dis- tinct experts, and we evaluate the consistency among these experts on the basis of Fleiss’s κ (refs. 37,38), which is an unsupervised meas- urement for assessing the agreement between independent raters. Having confirmed consensus among our experts, we draw the final expert label of each paper from the three experts according to the principle of the minority obeying the majority. We regard the expert labels as ground truth and validate the result of our BERT model against them with the F1-score, which is a supervised measurement of accuracy. Determine the project leader of papers Here we define the project leader as the last author of a research paper, in alignment with conventions established by previous studies59. To ensure that in most papers, the last author represents the project leader, we examine the fraction of papers that list authors following alphabetical order. First, we directly traverse all selected papers and obtain the prevalence of papers listing authors in alphabetical order, which ranges from 14.87% in materials science to 22.15% in geology. Nevertheless, it is difficult to distinguish whether these papers actu- ally intended to list the authors in alphabetical order or according to their roles, which unintentionally fall in alphabetical order. The latter situation is more likely to occur when there are fewer authors (two or three). To tackle this analytical challenge, we determine the fraction of unintended alphabetical author lists through a Monte Carlo method. We generate ten randomly shuffled copies of the author list for each paper and find that from 13.82% (materials science, σ = 0.02) to 20.28% (geology, σ = 0.03) of papers have alphabetically listed authors among the random author lists. This indicates the proportion of ‘unintended’ alphabetical author lists, and we can derive the actual fraction of papers with intentionally alphabetical author lists by the difference between the above two sets of statistical results. The actual fraction obtained illustrates that only 1.58% of papers across all disciplines intentionally list the authors in alphabetical order (Supplementary Table 12) and therefore, we can, with negligible interference, assume that we can identify last authors as team leaders. Detect scientists’ career role transition The OpenAlex dataset incorporates a well-designed author name dis- ambiguation mechanism29, which uses an XGBoost model60 to predict the likelihood that two authors are the same on the basis of features such as their institutions, co-authors and citations, and then applies a custom, ORCID-anchored clustering process to group their works, assigning a unique ID to each author. Simply using unique IDs, we are able to track a large number of authors at the same time61, where we depict an individual scientist’s career trajectory using a role transition model (Extended Data Fig. 4a) and extract the role transition trajecto- ries for scientists. First we traverse all selected papers in the six disciplines and extract all the scientists involved in any of these papers. Then, for each indi- vidual scientist, we extract all papers in which they have been involved and record the time of their first publication in any role, the time of their first publication as team leader (if ever), and the time of their last publication. We then filter out scientists whose publication records span only a single year. We also filter out those who directly start as established scientists leading research teams without a role transition from junior scientists. Finally, we detect the time that each scientist abandons academic publishing. Considering that one scientist may not publish papers continuously every year, we cannot regard them as having left academia on the basis of their absence in the published record for a single year. We therefore follow the settings used in pre- vious work62 to use a threshold of three years and regard scientists who have no more publications after 2022 as having exited academia, whereas those who still publish papers after 2022 are considered to have an unclear ultimate status and are excluded from the analysis. Finally, we obtain 2,282,029 scientists in the six disciplines with complete role transition trajectories. We also classify them into AI and non-AI scien- tists according to whether they have published AI-augmented papers. Moreover, by analysing author contribution statements collected in previous studies63,64, we further validate our detection results by examining changes in scientists’ self-reported contributions through- out their careers (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Results indicate that junior scientists primarily engage in technical tasks, such as conducting experiments and analysing data, and less in conceptual tasks, such as conceiving ideas and writing papers. Nevertheless, the proportion of conceptual work significantly rises (P < 0.01 and df = 1 in a Cochran– Armitage test) during their tenure as junior scientists, reaching satura- tion at a high level (60% or more) on transition to becoming established scientists. This finding validates our definition of role transition by demonstrating a shift in the nature of scientists’ contributions from participating in research projects to leading them. Estimate the birth–death model for career development of junior scientists To obtain a more precise quantification of how much AI acceler- ates the career development of junior scientists, we use a general birth–death model42. This type of stochastic process model depicts the dynamic evolution of a population as members join and exit. In our context, it models the role transitions of junior scientists. Spe- cifically, we use two separate birth–death models for junior scien- tists who eventually become established and for those who leave academia, respectively. This protocol was developed using brain and muscle tissues isolated from the Hsd:Sprague Dawley (SD) strain of Rattus norvegicus domestica subspecies. Materials 100 mg tissue (e.g. brain or muscle) 1X PBS pH 7.4 Crushed ice Liquid nitrogen Scalpel 15 or 50 ml centrifuge tubes Mortar and pestle –80°C freezer storage Cryo-grinding of animal tissues: 20 minutes hands-on-time Note: Pre-chill a mortar and pestle at –80°C for at least 30 minutes. Both fresh or frozen samples may be used. 1. Gather 100 mg of animal tissue. Note: If the material is >1 cm2, dissect the sample into smaller pieces before proceeding to the next step. 2. Place a chilled mortar and pestle on ice. Add a small volume of liquid nitrogen into the mortar and add the animal tissue to freeze until the liquid nitrogen has evaporated. 3. Carefully grind the frozen animal tissue into a fine powder, working quickly to minimise thawing. If the animal tissue starts to thaw, add a small volume of liquid nitrogen to the mortar. 4. Use a spatula to collect the tissue powder into a chilled centrifuge tube on ice RE-Pore-C extraction 1. Transfer approximately 100 mg of cryo-ground tissue to a 50 ml centrifuge tube and resuspend in 1 ml chilled 1X PBS. 2. Bring the volume of the re-suspended cryo-ground tissue to 10 ml in chilled 1X PBS. 3. Proceed with the RE-Pore-C protocol, using the re-suspended cryo-ground tissue powder as input. Management of Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia: Nonpharmacologic and Pharmacologic Interventions

Jennifer A. Watt, Zahinoor Ismail, Natasha Lane, Dallas Seitz, and Zahra Goodarzi Annual Review of Clinical Psychology, 2026, 22:397-425 First published as a Review in Advance on February 12, 2026 https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-clinpsy-061724-085912 Copyright © 2026 by the author(s). Licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

Abstract

Mounting evidence supports the efficacy of nonpharmacologic or psychosocial interventions for reducing behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), identifies the comparative risks and benefits of psychotropic medication, and underscores the importance of deprescribing psychotropic medications. However, evidence from clinical settings indicates that uptake of nonpharmacologic interventions and potential overuse of medications remain problematic. We begin by discussing the importance of exploring potential contributors to BPSD, using person-centered language to describe BPSD, implementing holistic and person-centered care plans, measuring clinically important changes in BPSD, and considering social determinants of health when assessing and managing BPSD; we also discuss the historical context informing how clinicians manage BPSD. Next, we compare and contrast nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic approaches to managing BPSD, evaluate their individual and comparative efficacy, and describe recommendations for intervention deprescribing or deimplementation. Lastly, we discuss strengths and limitations of the current evidence supporting BPSD management as well as recommendations for future research.

OVERVIEW

People with dementia manifest neuropsychiatric symptoms, commonly known as BPSD (behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia). BPSD manifest in all stages and types of dementia; 97% of people with dementia experience at least one BPSD within 5 years of diagnosis. Apathy, agitation, aggression, anxiety, irritability, depression, sleep and nighttime disturbances, aberrant motor behavior, disinhibition, appetite and eating changes, delusions, hallucinations, and euphoria can all be manifestations of BPSD.

We have an incomplete understanding of what causes BPSD, but personality, genetics, environmental factors, unmet needs, and anatomical and biochemical changes have been proposed as potential causes. BPSD are associated with greater cognitive and functional decline and heightened caregiver distress; clinicians and caregivers treat BPSD with nonpharmacologic interventions, medications, or both to alleviate the adverse outcomes associated with BPSD.

There is a growing body of literature describing the efficacy of pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions for BPSD management. However, the comparative efficacy of pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions is less well-described, and evidence informing how to best manage BPSD is evolving. Nonpharmacologic interventions can be broadly classified into four categories: psychological (e.g., reminiscence therapy), behavioral (e.g., modification of activities of daily living), sensory (e.g., aromatherapy), and environmental (e.g., outdoor activities). Some nonpharmacologic interventions can be classified into multiple categories or incorporate intervention components from multiple categories. Medications studied for treating BPSD include antipsychotics, antidepressants, anticonvulsants, cholinesterase inhibitors, N-methyl-d-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists (i.e., memantine), anxiolytics/hypnotics, and other drugs (e.g., dextromethorphan-quinidine, cannabinoids), although approaches vary widely.

Well-founded concerns about potential harms (e.g., all-cause mortality with antipsychotics) have led people with dementia, family and friend caregivers, and clinicians to search for safer approaches. Particularly attractive are holistic and person-centered BPSD management plans that aim to minimize medication-related harms by maximizing nonpharmacologic intervention use and deprescribing medications that are ineffective or harmful. Implementation of nonpharmacologic interventions for managing BPSD in routine clinical care is a critical ongoing challenge and focus of research.

EXPLORING MEANING IN BPSD TO INTEGRATE NONPHARMACOLOGIC INTERVENTIONS INTO CARE PLANS

How we care for and study people with dementia experiencing BPSD is situated within the person-centered dementia care model, with a goal to preserve personhood and dignity. Conceptual frameworks and empirical evidence describe how behavioral and psychological symptoms in people with dementia can have meaning. Personal (i.e., intrinsic to the individual), social, and environmental factors contribute to the well-being of people with dementia, thus influencing whether they respond to others in their environment to fulfill an unmet need or manifest psychological symptoms in response to how they feel.

Contributory factors include unmet needs for food, affection, or meaningful activity; experiences of pain; social stressors, such as communication difficulties between a person with dementia and their caregiver; and suboptimal environmental conditions, such as a room that is too hot or cold. Understanding the lifelong behavioral pattern of a person with dementia may also provide essential context for their current behavior.

Syntheses of empirical evidence demonstrate a causal association between participating in interventions that better align personal, social, and environmental factors with the needs of people with dementia and their caregivers and reduced BPSD. Multidisciplinary assessments with management plans reduce symptoms of agitation and depression in people with dementia. However, not all empirical studies have demonstrated a clinically meaningful improvement in BPSD associated with participating in tailored nonpharmacologic interventions. Thus, our current understanding of predisposing, protective, perpetuating, and precipitating factors for BPSD is incomplete, but both theoretical frameworks and empirical evidence suggest that at least some behavioral and psychological symptoms have meaning.

SHIFT TOWARD MORE INCLUSIVE LANGUAGE DESCRIBING BPSD

A variety of terminology is used to describe BPSD, including neuropsychiatric symptoms, behavioral changes, changed behaviors, responsive behaviors, and personal expressions. While the terminology for describing BPSD varies, the most common terms in clinical practice guidelines are BPSD and neuropsychiatric symptoms. BPSD are broken down into specific domains or symptom clusters. However, as there is greater adoption of the person-centered model of dementia care, a shift toward more person-centered language is emerging in the medical literature and at the point of care.

The person-centered language paradigm asserts that people with dementia are responding to a need, feeling, or their environment (i.e., responsive behaviors) and that language should be contextually appropriate and inclusive of people with dementia and their caregivers. Caregivers and people with dementia may prefer terminology that reflects the person-centered language paradigm as opposed to language used in the medical literature. Further, the person-centered language paradigm favors describing the nature of a behavior (e.g., describing how a person with dementia calls out requesting food as opposed to simply saying the person with dementia is agitated), which promotes development of nonpharmacologic interventions to meet the needs of people with dementia.

This divergence in terminology being applied in medical research and at the point of care creates challenges regarding how behavioral and psychological symptoms ought to be described, necessitating mapping of terms between these two paradigms when developing evidence-based care plans. Person-centered language also emphasizes describing behaviors (e.g., pacing, restless) rather than labeling an individual (e.g., they are aggressive). The challenge, however, lies with measurement; valid and reliable outcome measures, ideally based on a syndromic understanding of the behaviors operationalized with diagnostic criteria, are required to properly assess efficacy of interventions. Addressing this challenge is essential to enabling the use of nonpharmacologic approaches and reconciling disparate terminologies for behavioral changes in people with dementia.

NEED FOR PROACTIVE, TIERED, AND HOLISTIC BPSD ASSESSMENT AND MANAGEMENT APPROACHES

Holistic approaches for assessing people with BPSD are needed to understand the potential role of nonpharmacologic interventions, medications, or both in developing a care plan that recognizes and respects the personhood of an individual with dementia. Holistic approaches addressing potential protective, predisposing, perpetuating, and precipitating factors for BPSD require input from people with dementia, family or friend caregivers, and clinicians.

Care plans should not only be developed in reaction to observed behaviors and symptoms but also be proactive to prevent or lessen behavior and symptom burden. Further, tiered care plans support clinicians and family and friend caregivers to appropriately respond to changes in symptoms and behaviors (e.g., implement nonpharmacologic interventions before medications unless there is a risk of harm to self or others).

As an example, the DICE (describe, investigate, create, and evaluate) approach prompts clinicians to (a) contextualize and characterize the concerning behavior or psychological symptom; (b) investigate potential patient, caregiver, and environmental contributing factors; (c) collaborate with formal and informal caregivers to create a care plan that both addresses contributing factors and includes tiered, nonpharmacologic interventions before considering pharmacologic options; and (d) evaluate the effectiveness of the care plan.

A proactive, tiered, holistic, and co-created BPSD assessment and management approach aligns with person-centered dementia care models and has been associated with reductions in BPSD. Creating care plans co-created by multiple health disciplines, family or friend caregivers, and people with dementia (when possible) is crucial because understanding the meaning in behavior requires contextual information that can be provided only by those who know the person with dementia best.

Table 1: Factors to consider when assessing BPSD

Protective factors: - Presence of a familiar caregiver - Being in a familiar environment - Caregiver knowledge of dementia - Availability of support for caregivers - Use of glasses and hearing aids - Creation of a tailored dementia care plan that alerts carers to important predisposing, precipitating, and perpetuating factors for the person with dementia - Caregiver knowledge of person with dementia's preferred nonmedication interventions for reducing BPSD

Predisposing factors: - Over- or understimulating environment - Vision or hearing impairment - Comorbid psychiatric diagnoses - Worsening dementia severity - Caregiver burden or distress

Precipitating factors: - Pain - Hunger - Thirst - Medication changes - Feeling too hot or cold - Sleep disturbances

Perpetuating factors: - Poor communication strategies between carers and people with dementia - Inadequate identification and treatment of precipitating factor(s) - Inadequate implementation of the tailored dementia care plan - Lack of support for caregivers

MEASURING CLINICALLY IMPORTANT CHANGES IN BPSD

Measuring clinically important changes in BPSD is essential to determine whether interventions are effective. Outcome measures for BPSD include global measures that assess all neuropsychiatric symptoms, measures that target specific symptoms (e.g., agitation, depression), and measures that assess quality of life. Global measures of BPSD include the Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI), which is widely used in research and clinical practice.

The NPI assesses 12 neuropsychiatric symptom domains: delusions, hallucinations, agitation/aggression, depression/dysphoria, anxiety, elation/euphoria, apathy/indifference, disinhibition, irritability/lability, aberrant motor behavior, nighttime behavior disturbances, and appetite and eating changes. Each domain is assessed for frequency, severity, and caregiver distress. The NPI has been validated in multiple languages and is sensitive to change.

Measures targeting specific symptoms include scales such as the Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory (CMAI) for agitation, the Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia (CSDD) for depression, and the Apathy Evaluation Scale (AES) for apathy. These scales provide more detailed assessment of specific symptoms and may be more sensitive to change in those domains.

Goal attainment scaling is another approach to measuring clinically important change. This approach involves setting personalized goals with people with dementia and their caregivers and measuring progress toward those goals. This approach is particularly useful for assessing person-centered outcomes and may be more meaningful than standardized scales.

HEALTH EQUITY CONSIDERATIONS IN MANAGING BPSD

Social determinants of health influence the risk of developing dementia, the experience of BPSD, and access to appropriate care. Racial/ethnic differences in the presentation of BPSD have been observed, and cultural factors influence how behaviors are interpreted and managed. For example, some cultures may view certain behaviors as more or less problematic, influencing whether caregivers seek care and what interventions are considered acceptable.

Access to nonpharmacologic interventions may be limited by socioeconomic status, geographic location, and available resources. Rural communities may have fewer options for specialized dementia care and fewer trained personnel to implement nonpharmacologic interventions. Language barriers can also limit access to appropriate care and support.

Stigma surrounding dementia and mental health may vary across cultures and can influence help-seeking behaviors and treatment choices. Understanding these social determinants of health is essential for developing equitable approaches to BPSD assessment and management.

HISTORICAL CONTEXT OF BPSD MANAGEMENT

Historically, behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia were managed primarily with pharmacologic interventions, particularly antipsychotic medications. In the 1980s and 1990s, there was widespread use of typical and atypical antipsychotics to treat BPSD, despite limited evidence of efficacy and growing concerns about safety.

In the early 2000s, regulatory warnings highlighted the increased risk of mortality associated with antipsychotic use in older adults with dementia. These warnings led to increased scrutiny of antipsychotic prescribing and greater emphasis on nonpharmacologic approaches. However, antipsychotic use remains prevalent in many settings, particularly in long-term care facilities.

Recent guidelines and initiatives have emphasized the importance of person-centered care, nonpharmacologic interventions as first-line treatment, and careful evaluation of medication risks and benefits. The evolution of BPSD management reflects broader shifts toward more holistic and person-centered approaches to dementia care.

PHARMACOLOGIC AND NONPHARMACOLOGIC APPROACHES FOR BPSD

Agitation

Nonpharmacologic interventions for agitation include behavioral interventions, sensory interventions, environmental modifications, and psychological interventions. Music therapy has demonstrated efficacy for reducing agitation in people with dementia. Other effective interventions include caregiver education, structured activities, and environmental modifications to reduce overstimulation.

Pharmacologic options for agitation include atypical antipsychotics, antidepressants, and other medications. However, the evidence supporting pharmacologic interventions for agitation is limited, and the risk of harms (particularly with antipsychotics) is significant. Network meta-analyses have found that some nonpharmacologic interventions have similar or greater efficacy compared to pharmacologic interventions, with fewer adverse effects.

The DICE algorithm (Describe, Investigate, Create, Evaluate) provides a structured approach to managing agitation. This approach emphasizes understanding the meaning behind the behavior, addressing contributing factors, and implementing nonpharmacologic interventions before considering pharmacologic options.

Psychosis

Psychotic symptoms in dementia, including delusions and hallucinations, are challenging to manage. Nonpharmacologic approaches focus on environmental modifications, sensory interventions, and caregiver education. Understanding the meaning behind psychotic symptoms and addressing unmet needs can reduce their frequency and severity.

Pharmacologic options include atypical antipsychotics, which have modest efficacy for psychotic symptoms but carry significant risks. Pimavanserin, a selective serotonin inverse agonist, has been studied for dementia-related psychosis and may have a more favorable safety profile. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine may have modest benefits for psychotic symptoms, but the evidence is limited.

Depression

Depression in dementia is common and associated with poor outcomes. Nonpharmacologic interventions include psychotherapy, cognitive-behavioral therapy, exercise, and reminiscence therapy. Psychological interventions have demonstrated efficacy for reducing depressive symptoms in people with dementia.

Pharmacologic options include antidepressants, but the evidence for their efficacy is mixed. Meta-analyses have found modest benefits of antidepressants for depression in dementia, but the effect sizes are small and the risk of adverse effects is significant. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the most commonly prescribed class.

Anxiety

Anxiety symptoms in dementia are often overlooked but can significantly impact quality of life. Nonpharmacologic interventions include cognitive-behavioral therapy, relaxation techniques, and environmental modifications to reduce stress and anxiety. Psychological interventions have demonstrated efficacy for anxiety in people with dementia.

Pharmacologic options include antidepressants and benzodiazepines, but both have limited evidence and significant risks. Benzodiazepines are associated with falls, confusion, and worsening cognitive function, and their use should be minimized.

Apathy

Apathy is one of the most common neuropsychiatric symptoms in dementia but is often undertreated. Nonpharmacologic interventions include structured activities, exercise, and caregiver education to engage people with dementia in meaningful activities. Behavioral activation has demonstrated efficacy for reducing apathy.

Pharmacologic options include stimulants such as methylphenidate, which has shown modest efficacy in randomized controlled trials. However, the evidence is limited, and the risk of adverse effects must be carefully considered.

Sleep and Circadian Rhythm Disturbances

Sleep disturbances are common in dementia and significantly impact quality of life for people with dementia and their caregivers. Nonpharmacologic interventions include sleep hygiene education, light therapy, physical activity, and environmental modifications. Bright light therapy has demonstrated efficacy for improving sleep and reducing nighttime disturbances.

Pharmacologic options include melatonin, trazodone, and other sleep-promoting medications. However, the evidence is limited, and medications carry risks including falls, confusion, and daytime sedation. Trazodone is commonly used but has modest efficacy and significant adverse effects.

Inappropriate Sexual Behaviors

Inappropriate sexual behaviors are less common but can be distressing for caregivers and challenging to manage. Nonpharmacologic interventions focus on environmental modifications, caregiver education, and understanding the meaning behind the behavior. Evidence for effective interventions is limited.

Pharmacologic options include antipsychotics and other medications, but the evidence is extremely limited and the risks often outweigh benefits. Management typically focuses on nonpharmacologic approaches and addressing contributing factors.

Eating Disturbances

Eating disturbances in dementia include changes in appetite, food preferences, and eating behaviors. Nonpharmacologic interventions include nutritional assessment, environmental modifications to support eating, and caregiver education on feeding assistance. Understanding the meaning behind eating changes is important.

Pharmacologic options are limited and generally not recommended. Management focuses on addressing underlying causes such as dental problems, depression, or medication side effects. Nutritional supplementation may be considered in some cases.

Prescribing Cholinesterase Inhibitors or Memantine for BPSD

Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) and memantine are approved for cognitive symptoms of dementia but may have benefits for some BPSD. Meta-analyses have found modest benefits of cholinesterase inhibitors for some neuropsychiatric symptoms, but the evidence is mixed and the effect sizes are small.

These medications may be considered for BPSD, particularly when cognitive symptoms and BPSD co-occur. However, the benefits must be carefully weighed against the risks, and these medications should not be prescribed solely for BPSD in the absence of cognitive symptoms.

Is There a Role for New Alzheimer Disease–Modifying Therapies?

New disease-modifying therapies for Alzheimer disease, including lecanemab and donanemab, target amyloid-beta and have shown benefits for cognitive outcomes. Limited data are available on their effects on BPSD. As these therapies become more widely used, understanding their impact on neuropsychiatric symptoms will be important.

Risk of Harm Associated with Interventions for Treating BPSD

Antipsychotic medications are associated with significant harms in people with dementia, including increased mortality, stroke, falls, and cognitive decline. The number needed to harm for mortality with antipsychotics in dementia is approximately 26, meaning that for every 26 people treated, one additional death occurs.

Other psychotropic medications also carry risks. Antidepressants are associated with falls, gastrointestinal bleeding, and hyponatremia. Benzodiazepines are associated with falls, confusion, dependence, and cognitive decline. The risks of these medications must be carefully weighed against potential benefits.

Nonpharmacologic interventions generally have fewer risks than pharmacologic interventions, but they are not risk-free. Some interventions may cause overstimulation or understimulation, and poorly implemented interventions may fail to address the underlying causes of BPSD. However, overall, nonpharmacologic interventions have a more favorable safety profile than medications.

Deprescribing Pharmacologic Interventions and Deimplementing Nonpharmacologic Interventions

Deprescribing is the planned process of reducing or stopping medications that are no longer beneficial or where the harms outweigh the benefits. For BPSD, deprescribing should focus on antipsychotics and other psychotropic medications that may have been initiated without adequate trials of nonpharmacologic interventions.

Guidelines for deprescribing include gradual tapering, monitoring for withdrawal symptoms or recurrence of BPSD, and implementing nonpharmacologic interventions to support the deprescribing process. Successful deprescribing has been demonstrated in multiple settings, with reductions in antipsychotic use without worsening of BPSD.

Deimplementation of nonpharmacologic interventions refers to stopping interventions that are no longer beneficial or where the evidence does not support continued use. This process is less well-studied than deprescribing but is important to ensure resources are directed toward effective interventions.

INITIATIVES TO IMPROVE QUALITY OF CARE

Multiple initiatives have been developed to improve the quality of BPSD management. These include quality metrics for antipsychotic use in long-term care, educational programs for clinicians and caregivers, and implementation of evidence-based guidelines. These initiatives aim to reduce inappropriate medication use and increase the use of nonpharmacologic interventions.

STRENGTHS OF THE BODY OF LITERATURE SUPPORTING BPSD MANAGEMENT

The literature on BPSD management has several strengths. There is a growing body of randomized controlled trials evaluating both pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions. Network meta-analyses have compared the efficacy of different interventions, providing evidence to guide clinical decision-making. The literature has evolved from focusing primarily on pharmacologic interventions to giving greater attention to nonpharmacologic approaches and person-centered care.

LIMITATIONS OF THE BODY OF LITERATURE SUPPORTING BPSD MANAGEMENT

Despite the growing literature, there are important limitations. Many studies have methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, short follow-up periods, and heterogeneous outcome measures. The evidence for some interventions remains limited, and more research is needed to determine the optimal approaches for different BPSD and different populations. There is limited evidence on how to effectively implement nonpharmacologic interventions in routine clinical practice.

EMERGING AREAS OF RESEARCH ON BPSD MANAGEMENT

Emerging areas of research include digital health interventions, personalized medicine approaches to BPSD management, and implementation science to improve the uptake of evidence-based practices. There is growing interest in understanding the biological mechanisms underlying BPSD, which may lead to new targeted therapies. Telehealth and remote monitoring may improve access to BPSD assessment and management, particularly for underserved populations.

SUMMARY

BPSD are common in dementia and have significant impacts on people with dementia and their caregivers. There is growing evidence supporting the efficacy of nonpharmacologic interventions, which should be considered first-line treatment. Pharmacologic interventions, particularly antipsychotics, have limited efficacy and significant risks. Person-centered care approaches that understand the meaning behind behaviors and address contributing factors are essential for effective BPSD management. Future research should focus on improving the evidence base for specific interventions, understanding how to implement nonpharmacologic interventions in routine practice, and developing new approaches that are safe and effective.

docs.title: Arta overturns ato tax residency
docs.text: ARTA overturns ATO decision in tax residency case TAX The tribunal has found that the ATO incorrectly treated a taxpayer as an Australian tax resident only, in a case examining the tax treaty tie- breaker rules. 15 June 2026 • By Miranda Brownlee • 5 minutes read Share https://www.accountantsdaily.com.au/tax-compliance/22531-arta-overturns-ato-decision-in-tax-residency-case 19/6/2026, 12:24 Page 1 of 11 The case, Bulie and Commissioner of Taxation (Taxation) [2026] ARTA 1003, involved an applicant who was a dual resident of Australia and Singapore and had a permanent home and habitual abode in both countries. The main issue in the case was whether the applicant, Ragnar Bulie, was to be treated as a tax resident of Australia or Singapore for certain income years. Where someone is a resident under the domestic tax laws of both Singapore and Australia, the tax treaty between the two countries provides tie-breaker rules that determine which country the individual is treated as a resident of. The tribunal needed to determine which country Bulie's personal and economic relations were closest to. Login Become a free member Subscribe Register for a free account to access unlimited free content. Become a FREE member You have 4 free articles left this month. https://www.accountantsdaily.com.au/tax-compliance/22531-arta-overturns-ato-decision-in-tax-residency-case 19/6/2026, 12:24 Page 2 of 11 Between May 2019 and March 2023, the ATO issued a series of income tax assessments and Division 293 assessments in respect of Bulie's taxable employment income earned in Singapore for the income years ending 30 June 2018 through 30 June 2022 on the basis that Bulie was a tax resident of Australia. The assessments were based on the relevant income tax returns lodged by Bulie. Bulie lodged an objection to the assessments on 13 April 2024, contending that, under the treaty, he was to be treated as a tax resident of Singapore only during the relevant income years, meaning that his employment income was taxable only by Singapore. The ATO then disallowed the obligation in full in December 2024 on the basis that Bulie was to be treated as a tax resident of only Australia under the treaty tie-breaker rules. From January 2018 until the end of August 2022, Bulie lived in a leased residential property in Singapore. Since September 2022, he lived in another leased residential property in Singapore. Bulie's wife and youngest child have continued to live in the Sydney Home since 2013  Become a FREE member https://www.accountantsdaily.com.au/tax-compliance/22531-arta-overturns-ato-decision-in-tax-residency-case 19/6/2026, 12:24 Page 3 of 11 BY MACQUARIE GROUP SERVICES Work%ow e)iciency in the new AML/CTF landscape As Australia’s AML/CTF reforms bring Tranche 2 entities into a more rigorous compliance 3 MIN READ He spent 173 days physically present in Australia in 2018; 78 days in 2019; 189 days in 2020; 144 days in 2021; and 108 days in 2022. Overall, during these years, Bulie spent approximately 38 per cent of his time in Australia. In its decision, the Tribunal noted that Bulie earned the bulk of his income during the relevant period from his employment in Singapore. "As such, Singapore is the ‘centre of his day-to-day life and source of economic lifeline for himself and his family," said tribunal general member Micah Burch. The tribunal also said that while Bulie owned a home in Sydney, it was not an income- producing asset during the relevant periods and therefore did not alter Bulie's "actual, recurring economic activity which was centred in Singapore". It also gave little weight to Bulie's remaining economic ties to Australia, such as his https://www.accountantsdaily.com.au/tax-compliance/22531-arta-overturns-ato-decision-in-tax-residency-case 19/6/2026, 12:24 Page 4 of 11 maintaining private health cover, having Medicare access, and keeping bank accounts in Australia. "This is a function of the administrative realities and conveniences of dual residency and does not have a signiﬁcant bearing on the tie-breaker test in this case," said Burch. The tribunal found that Bulie's economic and personal relations with Singapore were, in the composite, stronger than his economic and personal relations with Australia during the relevant period. "During the Relevant Period, Mr Bulie spent the bulk of his time in Singapore and earned the bulk of his income in Singapore. Though his personal relations to Australia were stronger, he had meaningful personal relations in Singapore as well," Burch said. "And though his ownership of assets in Australia was not insigniﬁcant, they did not produce income and paled in their signiﬁcance when compared to the primacy of his income-earning activity in Singapore." The tribunal therefore found that Bulie's strongest personal and economic relations during the relevant period, when considered holistically, were with Singapore and that he had successfully discharged his burden of proving that the assessments from the ATO were incorrect. The tribunal set aside the decision on the objection and allowed Bulie's objection in full. Want to see more stories from trusted news sources? Make Accountants Daily a preferred news source on Google. docs.title: Australian tax residence guide
docs.text: https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 1 of 12 Understanding tax residency status for Tax Purposes in Australia May 29, 2026 Your tax residency status is one of the most consequential determinations the ATO will make about you. Get it right and you know exactly what you owe. Get it wrong and you could face unexpected bills, penalties, or miss out on offsets you were entitled to claim. The core issue is straightforward: Australian tax residents pay tax on their worldwide income. Non-residents pay tax only on income sourced within Australia. That single distinction can mean thousands of dollars of difference in your annual tax position, especially if you have overseas income, assets held abroad, or a period of working internationally. The Australian Taxation Office ( (https://www.ato.gov.au/) ATO ) uses a series of statutory tests to determine where you sit. Understanding those tests, and how they apply to your personal circumstances, is the starting point for getting this right. What Is the Importance of Tax Residency Status? Tax residency status determines the full scope of your Australian tax obligations. Residents are assessed on all income, regardless of where in the world it was earned. That includes salary from a foreign employer, rental income from an overseas property, and returns from international investments. Non-residents face a narrower obligation but are generally taxed at higher rates on their Australian-sourced income, and they lose access to the tax-free threshold. So while a non- resident might owe no Australian tax on foreign income, they will pay more on whatever they do earn here. Residency status also affects your eligibility for the Medicare levy, the foreign income tax offset, and certain capital gains tax concessions. For anyone moving to Australia, leaving the country, or splitting time between two jurisdictions, getting the right classification early avoids compounding problems at lodgement time. The tax (https://www.bentleys.com.au) accountants at Bentleys https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 2 of 12 regularly help clients work through these questions, particularly where the facts are complex or the outcome is disputed. Key Tests for Determining Your Tax Residency Status The ATO does not rely on a single test to classify your residency. It applies to up to four statutory tests in sequence. If you satisfy any one of them, you are an Australian tax resident for that financial year. The tests are the Resides Test (the primary test), the Domicile Test, the 183-Day Test, and the Commonwealth Superannuation Test. Each looks at different aspects of your connection to Australia, from your lifestyle and living arrangements to your physical presence and employment status. They work independently. Failing one does not prevent you from satisfying another. The Resides Test The Resides Test is the starting point and asks a basic question: does this person live in Australia? The answer requires more than counting nights spent here. The ATO looks at the totality of your circumstances to decide whether Australia is genuinely where you reside. Factors considered include where your family lives, where you are employed, whether you own or rent property in Australia, your participation in community or social activities, and how regularly you return here. No single factor is determinative. Someone who splits their time between Australia and another country might still pass the Resides Test if the weight of their personal and economic ties is firmly here. If the Resides Test is satisfied, you are a resident. If it is not, the ATO moves to the remaining tests. The Domicile Test for Tax The Domicile Test applies where someone does not appear to reside in Australia in the ordinary sense but may still have Australia as their permanent home. It is particularly relevant for Australians living or working overseas temporarily, such as those on an expatriate assignment or posted abroad for work. https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 3 of 12 Under the Domicile Test, you are an Australian tax resident if your domicile (your permanent home) is in Australia, unless the ATO is satisfied that your permanent place of abode is outside Australia. That last qualification matters. If you have moved overseas and established a genuine long-term home there, the Domicile Test may not catch you, even if you were born in Australia or hold an Australian passport. Property ownership, family ties, where your assets are held, and the duration and intent of your overseas stay all feed into this assessment. The 183-Day Rule Australia The 183-Day Test provides a more mechanical trigger. Spend 183 days or more in Australia during a financial year and you will generally be classified as a tax resident for that year, even without any intention of making Australia your permanent home. The count runs across the full financial year (1 July to 30 June). Days of arrival and departure are typically counted as full days. The test can catch people who have been in Australia on an extended work project, even without any plan to stay permanently. There is an exception. If you can demonstrate that your usual place of abode is outside Australia and you had no intention of taking up residence here, the 183-day count alone may not be enough to classify you as a resident. But this exception is applied narrowly. If you are spending that much time in Australia, the ATO will examine your circumstances closely. The Permanent Place of Abode The Permanent Place of Abode test runs alongside the Domicile Test rather than operating as a standalone measure. It is the mechanism that prevents someone from being treated as an Australian tax resident purely because their domicile is here, where they have genuinely established a long-term home overseas. To satisfy this exemption, your overseas home must be more than temporary accommodation. A short-term rental while on contract work abroad would generally not qualify. A home you have bought, furnished, and settled into with your family, with no immediate intention to return to Australia, is more likely to meet the standard. Factors the ATO considers include the duration of your overseas stay, whether you have sold or rented out your Australian property, where your spouse and children are living, and whether you maintain social and financial ties within Australia. https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 4 of 12 The Commonwealth Superannuation Test The Commonwealth Superannuation Test is a narrow test that applies only to Australian government employees posted overseas. If you are a member of the Public Sector Superannuation Scheme, the Commonwealth Superannuation Scheme, or a similar government fund, and you are working abroad, you may be classified as an Australian tax resident under this test regardless of your physical location. The policy reasoning is sensible. Government employees working overseas are there at the direction of the Australian Government, not because they have chosen to relocate. Treating them as non-residents would create inconsistencies relative to colleagues working within Australia. Government employees and contractors should take advice on how this test interacts with their broader tax position, including superannuation planning. Bentleys’ (https://www.bentleys.com.au/services/tax-advisory/) tax advisors work with clients in both public and private sectors on these cross-border arrangements. Special Cases and Exemptions Working Holiday Makers Working holiday makers, those who hold a subclass 417 or 462 visa, are taxed at a flat rate on their Australian income rather than the progressive rates applied to residents. From the 2017 financial year onwards, that rate has been 15% on the first $45,000 of taxable income, with ordinary non-resident rates applying above that threshold. Working holiday makers are generally treated as non-residents for tax purposes, regardless of how many days they spend in Australia, and they do not have access to the tax-free threshold. Temporary Residents Temporary residents enjoy a partial exemption from Australian tax. If you hold a temporary visa and are not the spouse of an Australian citizen or permanent resident, you are generally taxed only on your Australian-sourced income and employment income attributable to your time here. Most foreign income, including overseas interest, dividends, and capital gains from foreign assets, is excluded from your assessable Australian income. The temporary resident regime is a deliberate concession, recognising that people here on a provisional basis have not fully committed to the country and should not carry the same tax obligations as someone who has settled permanently. https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 5 of 12 Part-Year Residency If your residency status changes during a financial year, different rules apply to each segment of the year. When you become an Australian tax resident, you are assessed as a resident from that date. When you cease to be a resident, non-resident treatment applies from that point. The ATO has specific guidance on how to handle income allocation and asset disposal timing in these situations, and getting the timing right can have a meaningful effect on your tax bill. The Impact of Tax Residency on Your Taxes The headline impact is straightforward. Residents pay tax on global income at progressive Australian rates, the rate for 2025-26 is 16 cents in the dollar on income from $18,201 to $45,000, following the Stage 3 tax cuts that took effect from 1 July 2024. Non-residents pay no Australian tax on foreign income but face higher flat rates on Australian income, with no tax- free threshold applying. The Medicare levy (currently 2% of taxable income) applies to residents but not non-residents. Higher-income residents without private hospital cover may also face the Medicare levy surcharge. For capital gains tax purposes, non-residents are only subject to CGT on “taxable Australian property”, primarily Australian real estate and interests in entities with predominantly real property assets. The 50% CGT discount that residents can access after holding an asset for 12 months is generally not available to foreign residents. These differences add up quickly. For someone with significant global income or a large property portfolio, the resident/non-resident distinction could mean tens of thousands of dollars per year. It is also worth noting that withholding tax obligations can arise when Australian entities make payments such as interest, dividends, or royalties to foreign residents. Bentleys’ (https://www.bentleys.com.au/client-alert-tax-news-september-2024/) September 2024 client alert on withholding for foreign residents explains these obligations in more detail, including when exemptions might apply. Double Taxation Agreements and Foreign Income Tax Offset Australia has signed double taxation agreements (DTAs) with over 40 countries. These agreements allocate taxing rights over specific income types so that the same income is not taxed in full by two countries simultaneously. DTAs commonly cover salary, dividends, royalties, pensions, and capital gains, specifying which country has the primary right to tax each type and at what rate. https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 6 of 12 If you are an Australian resident who has already paid tax overseas on foreign income, you may be able to claim the foreign income tax offset (FITO) to reduce your Australian tax liability. The offset is generally capped at the lesser of the foreign tax paid and the Australian tax that would otherwise be payable on that income. It removes double taxation without resulting in a refund exceeding what you paid abroad. DTAs can also assist with residency determination itself. Some agreements include tie-breaker rules that determine which country a person is a tax resident of when both countries would otherwise claim them. If you are living or working in a DTA country and your residency status is uncertain, the relevant agreement is worth examining carefully. The (https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/coming-to-australia-or-going-overseas/your-tax-residency) ATO’s guidance on tax residency for individuals includes information on how DTAs interact with the Australian tests. Tax Residency Self-Assessment Australia operates on a self-assessment basis. You determine your own tax residency status, and you are responsible for the accuracy of that determination. The ATO does not pre-approve your classification before you lodge your return. That creates a genuine record-keeping obligation. If you are claiming non-residency, you should be able to document your time spent outside Australia, your overseas living arrangements, and the nature of your ties to other countries. Travel records, lease agreements, employment contracts, and bank statements are all potentially relevant. The ATO does audit residency claims and tends to scrutinise arrangements that look contrived. A common mistake is assuming that simply being outside Australia for a period makes you a non-resident, particularly where you have maintained a home here, kept your family in Australia, or continued to earn Australian income. If your circumstances are anything other than clear-cut, seeking advice before lodgement is a better investment than addressing an ATO amendment after the fact. Residency Status Impact on Tax Rates For most people, the difference in tax rates between residents and non-residents is material. Residents have access to offsets, deductions, and concessions, including the low income tax offset and the seniors and pensioners tax offset, that non-residents cannot claim. Residents also benefit from the tax-free threshold and access to the CGT discount on eligible assets. https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 7 of 12 For those in a borderline situation, getting the classification right matters in both directions. Claiming non-resident status when you are actually a resident creates a risk of penalties and interest if the ATO disagrees. Claiming resident status when you are actually a non-resident could mean overpaying tax unnecessarily. Bentleys’ (https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/international-tax-guide-for-foreign-companies-doing-business-in- australia/) guide to international tax for individuals and foreign companies explores how Australian tax rates and obligations apply across different residency classifications and business structures. Where to Go From Here Tax residency is not a set-and-forget classification. Your status can change when you leave Australia, return from overseas, change employment, sell property, or alter your living arrangements significantly. Reviewing your position whenever there is a material change in your circumstances keeps you ahead of any problems. If you are confident in your classification, keep documentation that would support it through an audit. If there is any uncertainty, professional advice before lodgement is cheaper and less stressful than dealing with an ATO review after the fact. The (https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/coming-to-australia-or-going-overseas/your-tax-residency) ATO’s residency determination too l is a useful starting point for straightforward cases. For anything involving multiple countries, foreign assets, or recent changes in your living arrangements, a conversation with a specialist tax adviser will give you considerably more certainty. Disclaimer: This information is general in nature and should not be relied on as advice. It does not take into account the objectives, financial situation or needs of any particular person. You need to consider your financial situation and needs and seek professional advice before making any decisions based on this information. FAQs Am I an Australian resident for tax purposes? https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 8 of 12 You are generally considered an Australian resident for tax purposes if you satisfy at least one of the ATO’s residency tests, including the resides test, domicile test, 183-day test, or Commonwealth superannuation test. What is the difference between tax residency and immigration status? Tax residency is separate from immigration status. You can be a temporary visa holder but still be an Australian tax resident, or hold permanent residency while remaining a foreign resident for tax purposes. How does the resides test work in Australia? The resides test examines whether you live in Australia according to ordinary concepts, considering factors such as family ties, lifestyle, work arrangements, and where your assets are located. What is the 183-day test for Australian tax? If you spend 183 days or more in Australia during a financial year, you may be considered a tax resident unless your usual place of abode is overseas and you do not intend to reside in Australia. Do I need to pay tax on my worldwide income as an Australian resident? Yes, Australian tax residents generally must declare all worldwide income, including overseas salary, investments, and foreign rental income. What are the tax rates for foreign residents in Australia? For the 2025–26 financial year, foreign residents are taxed at 30 per cent up to $135,000, 37 per cent between $135,001 and $190,000, and 45 per cent above $190,000. Is there a tax-free threshold for Australian tax residents? Yes, Australian residents receive the standard tax-free threshold of $18,200, though this may be adjusted for part-year residency. What is the domicile test for Australian residency? You may be considered a resident if your legal domicile is in Australia unless you establish a permanent place of abode outside Australia. https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 9 of 12 What constitutes a permanent place of abode outside Australia? The ATO generally looks for a settled, long-term overseas living arrangement with continuity and permanence rather than temporary accommodation. How does being a temporary resident affect my Australian tax? Temporary residents are generally only taxed on Australian-sourced income and are exempt from tax on most foreign income. Do working holiday makers count as Australian residents? Most working holiday makers are taxed under special rates starting at 15 per cent on the first $45,000 of Australian income regardless of residency status. How is the financial year defined for Australian tax residency? The Australian financial year runs from 1 July to 30 June, and residency tests are applied across this period. Does owning property in Australia make me a tax resident? Owning property alone does not determine residency, though it is one factor the ATO considers when assessing your overall circumstances. What is the Commonwealth superannuation test? This test applies to certain Australian Government employees and members of eligible Commonwealth superannuation schemes working overseas. Can I be a resident of two countries for tax purposes? Yes, dual residency is possible. In these cases, double taxation agreements usually contain tie- breaker rules to determine which country has primary taxing rights. Do foreign residents pay the Medicare levy? Foreign residents are generally exempt from the Medicare levy if they are not entitled to Medicare benefits. What happens if my residency status changes mid-year? https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 10 of 12 You may become a part-year resident, meaning different tax rules apply to different portions of the financial year. Is a holiday house in Australia considered a permanent place of abode? Generally not. Holiday homes usually lack the permanence and continuity required to establish residency for tax purposes. How does the ATO view short-term work contracts for residency? Short-term contracts alone do not automatically create residency, especially if you maintain stronger personal and financial ties overseas. Does the 183-day test apply to a calendar year? No, the test applies specifically to the Australian financial year from 1 July to 30 June. Will my overseas student debt affect my residency status? No, HELP or student debt does not determine residency, though Australian residents living overseas must still report worldwide income for repayment purposes. Do I need to inform the ATO when I leave Australia permanently? Yes, you should notify the ATO when your residency status changes, often through your final Australian tax return. How is Capital Gains Tax (CGT) applied to foreign residents? Foreign residents are generally only taxed on gains relating to taxable Australian property, such as Australian real estate. Can I use the ATO residency tool for a definitive answer? The ATO residency tool provides guidance only. Complex cases often require advice from a qualified Australian tax professional. Are there new residency laws coming to Australia? The Government has proposed reforms to modernise residency tests, though the current four statutory tests remain in force as of 2026. https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 11 of 12 Does spending 183 days in Australia automatically make me a resident? Not automatically. You may still argue that your usual place of abode remains overseas and that you had no intention of residing permanently in Australia. Are temporary residents taxed on their foreign income? Generally, no. Most foreign investment income earned by temporary residents is excluded from Australian assessable income. What happens if my residency status changes partway through the year? A split-year treatment applies, meaning different tax rules and thresholds apply to resident and non-resident periods separately. Does tax residency match my visa or immigration status? No, Australian tax residency is determined independently from immigration law and is based on the statutory residency tests applied by the ATO. https://www.bentleys.com.au/insights/understanding-tax-residency-status-for-tax-purposes-in-australia/ 19/6/2026, 12:29 Page 12 of 12

docs.title: Brain tissue dna extraction method
docs.text: OXFORD NANOPORE Extracting and preparing DNA from brain tissue for Oxford Nanopore Sequencing FOR RESEARCH USE ONLY OXFORD NANOPORE TECHNOLOGIES | Extracting and preparing DNA from brain tissue for Oxford Nanopore Sequencing PAGE 1 Contents Introduction Materials Method 1. Tissue lysis 2. DNA extraction 3. DNA shearing Results OXFORD NANOPORE TECHNOLOGIES | Extracting and preparing DNA from brain tissue for Oxford Nanopore Sequencing PAGE 2 Introduction This protocol describes a method to extract genomic DNA from human brain tissue using the QIAGEN MagAttract HMW DNA Kit and can be automated by using the KingFisher Flex or Duo Prime systems using the MagAttract handbook for these systems. This extraction method recovers ~8-15 µg of DNA from 25 mg of human brain tissue. Sequencing libraries were prepared using the Ligation Sequencing Kit both with and without a high throughput DNA shearing step using the FastPrep-96, before sequencing on PromethION Flow Cells. Flow cell output was increased by washing the flow cell using the Flow Cell Wash Kit and re-loading prepared library. Materials 25 mg of frozen brain tissue Ligation Sequencing Kit QIAGEN MagAttract HWM DNA Kit Scalpel Weighing boats 1 ml 96-well plates Plate sealer (e.g. Bio-Rad PX1 PCR plate sealer) Pierceable Foil Heat Seals 2 ml DNA LoBind Eppendorf Tubes P1000 pipette and tips P1000 wide-bore tips Weighing scales capable of measuring 25 mg Thermomixer Magnetic rack FastPrep (e.g. FastPrep-96 Classic bead beating grinder and lysis system) Optional materials QIAGEN TissueRuptor II 15 ml Falcon Tube Agilent Femto Pulse System Femto Pulse System DNA Analysis Kit (e.g. Genomic DNA 165 kb Kit) Method Tissue lysis Brain tissue should always be kept frozen prior to processing the sample. Please note, when the frozen sample is sliced, it will thaw quickly and generate condensation around the tissue, which will affect the weight. Please take the necessary precautions depending on the type and origin of the tissues you are working with. 1. Use a scalpel to thinly slice 25 mg of frozen brain tissue and place in a sterile weighing boat. 2. Homogenise the tissue to ensure adequate penetration of the lysis buffer into the tissue to accelerate the lysis step. This can be performed in one of two ways: OXFORD NANOPORE TECHNOLOGIES | Extracting and preparing DNA from brain tissue for Oxford Nanopore Sequencing PAGE 3 Recommended: Use a scalpel to mince the brain tissue in a weighing boat until it turns into a paste-like consistency which should take several minutes. Transfer the minced tissue into a 2 ml DNA LoBind Eppendorf Tube or 1 ml 96-well plate. Add 400 µl of MagAttract Lysis buffer (ATL) (MagAttract HMW DNA Kit) and 40 µl of proteinase K to the sample immediately. To ensure even dispersion through the sample, slowly mix by pipetting, using a P1000 pipette and standard P1000 tip approximately 5 times until the tissue is homogenised in the solution. Alternative (using TissueRuptor): Place 25 mg of sliced tissue in a 15 ml Falcon Tube and add 400 µl of MagAttract Lysis buffer (ATL). Shear the sample for 2 seconds at minimum speed in the TissueRuptor. Add 40 µl of proteinase K to the sample. 3. Place the tubes or 96-well plate in a thermomixer preheated to 56°C and shake at 1000 rpm for 1 hour. 4. Remove the samples from the thermomixer. Note: The tissue should be completely or almost completely dissolved. If not, it is possible the tissue was not properly broken down in the previous step. To dissolve any intact tissue, pipette mix the tissue using a P1000 pipette tip to break up any tissue aggregates and incubate for another 30-60 minutes. If some small pieces of tissue are still visible in solution after the lysis incubation, precipitate these by centrifuging at 16,000 x g for 3 minutes and remove any supernatant without disturbing the pellet. This is important as any undissolved pieces of tissue may bind to the MagAttract beads which can be very difficult to remove. 5. Take forward the homogenate to extract the DNA using a modified version of the QIAGEN MagAttract protocol. DNA extraction Note: This is a modified version of the QIAGEN Magattract HMW DNA protocol. 1. Add 8 µl of RNase and mix gently by flicking the tube. 2. Incubate at room temperature for 2 minutes. 3. Add 300 µl of AL buffer and mix using a P1000 wide-bore pipette 5-10 times. 4. Add 560 µl of MB buffer followed by 60 µl of MagAttract beads. Thoroughly resuspend by vortexing for 2-3 seconds. If using a 96-well plate, cover with adhesive film or use a plate sealer. 5. Incubate in a thermomixer for 3 minutes at 1000 rpm at room temperature. 6. Place the plate/tube on a magnet to pellet the magnetic beads. Remove the supernatant by pipetting without disturbing the bead pellet. 7. Add 700 µl of MW1 and resuspend the beads. 8. Use a thermomixer to mix the reaction for 2 minutes at 1000 rpm at room temperature. 9. Place the plate/tube on a magnet to pellet the magnetic beads. Remove the supernatant by pipetting without disturbing the bead pellet. 10. Repeat steps 7, 8 and 9 to complete a second wash with MW1. 11. Pre-warm Buffer AE to 80°C. 12. Add 700 µl of Buffer PE to the bead pellet. 13. Use a thermomixer to mix the reaction for 2 minutes at 1000 rpm at room temperature. 14. Place the plate/tube on a magnet to pellet the magnetic beads. Remove the supernatant by pipetting without disturbing the bead pellet. 15. Repeat steps 12, 13 and 14 to complete a second wash with Buffer PE. 16. Resuspend the beads with 150-200 µl Buffer AE, which has been pre-heated to 80°C, to elute the DNA. 17. Use a thermomixer to mix for 1 hour at 600 rpm at 37°C. 18. Place the plate/tube on a magnet to pellet the magnetic beads. Retain the supernatant containing the eluted DNA. 19. Quantify the recovered DNA using a Qubit fluorometer. OXFORD NANOPORE TECHNOLOGIES | Extracting and preparing DNA from brain tissue for Oxford Nanopore Sequencing PAGE 4 DNA shearing 1. After recovering and quantifying the elution from the MagAttract beads, transfer the eluate into a new 1 ml 96-well plate. It is important to keep the volumes used in this shearing method constant as different volumes and different plates may have an impact on shearing performance. It is also advisable to avoid the formation of bubbles when transferring the DNA sample as bubbles may effect the shearing and impact the final output. Note: We recommend the plates are thoroughly sealed using a heat sealer and appropriate seal. 2. Place the sealed plate in the FastPrep-96. 3. Shear at 1200 rpm for 1 minute. 4. Remove the plate and spin down to make sure no liquid is left in the seal. 5. Optional: Evaluate the shearing by analysing an aliquot before and after shearing using an Agilent Femto Pulse (or equivalent for QC). 6. After the extraction and shearing step, proceed with the library preparation protocol for the Ligation Sequencing Kit. Results Figure 1. a) Read length analysis, b) output analysis and c) Femto Pulse analysis of sheared and unsheared gDNA extracted from human brain samples.
