00:00 8 am. April 2, 1912. The magisterial ship the  Titanic leaves the Belfast dock for sea trials.

00:06 Thousands of people have come to watch,

00:08 waving their handkerchiefs in the  air and shouting “Rule Britannia”.

00:12 Some of them chase the ship down the  slipway as she slowly moves away.

00:15 Not one of them could ever expect  that such a behemoth of a vessel

00:19 would end up at the bottom of the icy-cold ocean,  dragging countless people to the depths with it.

00:24 April 10, 1912. On a cold morning, Captain  Edward John Smith arrives at the Southampton dock

00:30 where his crew has been sleeping  on the Titanic through the night.

00:33 Smith is a confident man, and proud of  British shipbuilding expertise. Prior to

00:37 his heading the Titanic he’d told a reporter: “Whatever happens, there will be time enough

00:41 before the vessel sinks to save the life of  every person on board. I will go a bit further.

00:45 I will say that I cannot imagine any condition  that would cause the vessel to founder.”

00:49 Oh, how wrong could he be! We’ll talk  a lot about this guy as things go on.

00:53 Later in the morning, Fifth Officer Harold  Lowe and Sixth Officer James Moody are there

00:58 to supervise a lifeboat drill, unfortunately,  the only one that would happen on the Titanic.

01:02 As midday approaches, the passengers arrive:  rich, poor, and something in between. The ship

01:07 can take 2,453 passengers: 833 in first class,  614 in second class, and 1,006 in third class,

01:16 but there will only be about 2,200  passengers on board when the thing goes down.

01:20 The wealthy board from one entrance and the poor  at another entrance. Those with meager means are

01:25 the third-class passengers, who on arrival are  checked for an eye disease called trachoma.

01:30 The USA doesn’t want these folks, but only  one person it seems is turned away. Lucky him!

01:35 About a third of third-class, dreaming of a new  life in the US, are not native English speakers.

01:40 Their basic cabins reflect their status,  or class, as the British like to call it.

01:44 These are people who will suffer the worst,  screaming in their native tongues as they slide

01:48 down the deck of a ship turning upwards towards  the sky. Some are Bulgarian, Syrian, Italian,

01:54 Swedish, and Russian; some are even Chinese,  even though the Chinese Exclusion Act in the US

01:59 means Chinese laborers aren’t  welcome in the country.

02:02 The first-class passengers enter their  beautiful cabins. These are the bankers,

02:06 businessmen, military leaders, socialites,  athletes, American millionaires,

02:10 and the ever-snooty British aristocracy.

02:12 This is the who’s who of wealthy society,

02:14 and many have arrived with personal  nurses, valets, chefs, and chauffeurs.

02:18 On the ship, they’ll enjoy Turkish  baths, a gymnasium, a squash court,

02:22 a saltwater swimming pool, and even first-class  kennels for their beloved pooches. For their trip,

02:27 and ultimately their death, some of them have  paid around 90,000 bucks in today’s money.

02:32 The second-class passengers: professionals,  academics, religious men, and tourists,

02:37 don’t quite get such luxuries,  but their cabins aren’t too bad.

02:40 It goes without saying that all three classes  will not dine together. They are separated,

02:43 and will only really come together when they are  faced with the matter of life or death. Today,

02:48 these third-class folks will eat rabbit pie,  potatoes, bread and butter, and some rhubarb

02:52 and ginger jam for dessert. The first-class  passengers will devour a 13-course meal,

02:57 including foie gras, peaches in chartreuse  jelly, and a helping of Waldorf pudding.

03:02 It’s early evening on April 10 when  the ship leaves Cherbourg in France

03:06 and heads to Queenstown, Ireland. Some of the  working-class kids are playing on the baggage

03:10 cranes while their parents play cards in the  common room. Life isn’t bad at all on this ship,

03:14 say some of the guys while smoking in  the smoking room - no women allowed!

03:18 As night falls, the upper classes are  already light-headed on champagne,

03:22 talking of their business ventures and mansion  renovations as semi-royal Brits whisper together

03:27 about how vulgar in style and speech one certain  fabulously wealthy American industrialist is.

03:32 They can at least be assured that none of them  will bump into another class, with grilles all

03:36 over the ship that separates the rich and poor. Midday, April 11, and the ship finally arrives

03:42 in Ireland. Many of the wealthy passengers have  just woken up with sore heads, staring down at

03:47 Norwegian salmon and poached eggs. The poor  for the most part have been up since sunrise.

03:51 About 2 pm more passengers board, and the Titanic  is off again. It’s about to get very cold.

03:57 As the ship heads West over the Atlantic,  the captain looks out into the distance.

04:00 The weather is good. The passengers are all  safely on board. So far, he hasn’t given much

04:05 time to the fact that among his crew only about 5  percent are able seamen. Most of the others have

04:10 regular day jobs such as firemen, and little  do they know about the many perils of sailing.

04:15 On April 12, while merriment is being  had by many on board, the morning is

04:19 a wonderful thing to see. The skies are clear,  and the Atlantic is uncharacteristically calm.

04:24 During the afternoon, two young working-class  kids scream for joy as they play hide and seek,

04:29 while America’s first multi-millionaire, the real  estate tycoon and opium smuggler John Jacob Astor,

04:34 talks with the Titanic’s  architect, Thomas Andrews.

04:38 “Is it sinkable,” asks Astor with a smile  on his face. This man is so rich, richer in

04:43 relative terms than any person today, he probably  thinks he’s invincible. Andrews returns the smile,

04:48 answering, “This ship even the great  Poseidon couldn’t sink.” Both men laugh out

04:53 loud as American silent film actress Dorothy  Gibson walks over to see what’s so amusing.

04:58 Both of these men will soon be dead. Gibson  will survive. Women and children first,

05:02 that’s how things will go, although some  men will try their luck. But for now,

05:06 all is perfect, and for two days, life  aboard the Titanic couldn’t be any better.

05:10 As the evening of April 13 turns into the night  and the band plays under a blanket of stars,

05:15 the conditions couldn’t be any better. About  9.30 pm, Captain Smith retires to his cabin,

05:20 his job done for the day. He’s not  aware that the Titanic is about to

05:24 sail under an arctic high-pressure system. In the morning things are not so fine and

05:28 dandy. Around 9 am, senior wireless operator  Jack Phillips is informed by other vessels

05:33 that to the West there are icebergs. The liner  named the Carolina tells him to watch out for

05:37 the hard-to-see Growlers, smaller icebergs  that can still pose a danger to a large ship.

05:42 At 10 am Captain Smith tells his men they  needn’t bother with the lifeboat drill,

05:46 even though he’s been told about  those floating fortresses of ice.

21:00 facts wrong at these rates would not

21:10 is the technology, who on earth is

22:03 haven't heard much about them in the AI

22:26 Street's AI is wrong, the market tells

22:49 revolution so far are companies that

00:00 We’ve been told pandemics are biological  accidents that take years to emerge.

00:05 But what if that’s wrong? New evidence suggests

00:08 something far more unsettling. The next  global killer is already out there,

00:12 waiting and it’s pre-programmed  to hijack your cells right now.

00:15 What if there was never a missing  link in COVID’s origin story?

00:19 Not because of a conspiracy. But because  the virus may never have needed to evolve

00:23 to infect us in the first place. It was born with the master key.

00:27 And if that's true, we're not waiting  for the next pandemic to evolve…

00:31 we're waiting for it to arrive.

00:33 From the very first day of existence, humanity  has had to navigate a biological minefield.

00:37 We knew that there were viruses out there,  invisible to the naked eye. We knew they had

00:42 the potential to wreak havoc inside our bodies  and even bring our lives to an early end.

00:46 We thought we had a certain level of safety. For years - generations, even - public health

00:52 policies, vaccine strategies, and  pandemic response systems were all

00:55 based on a single and important assumption.  That there is a buffer between us and the

01:00 viruses that could potentially wipe us all out. We believed that microbes essentially followed a

01:05 pre-programmed, step-by-step route. First, those viruses would spread

01:08 through that animal population before  eventually jumping into another species,

01:12 like a pangolin, a pig or maybe a civet. And that's where things began to change.

01:17 Inside these new hosts, the  virus would start changing.

01:20 Each infection created new copies. Each new  copy was another chance for a mistake. Another

01:25 mutation. Most went nowhere. But over time,  those mutations could stack up. And eventually,

01:30 the virus might stumble onto the exact  tools it needed to infect humans.

01:35 That’s when we’d need to worry. Once they gained the ability to infect humans,

01:38 they could spread from person to person. As they  moved through the population, they could trigger

01:43 powerful immune responses that make us sick. At  best, that means pain, fever, and discomfort.

01:48 At worst, it can cost lives. Scientists called this buffer the species barrier.

01:53 It was the idea that animal viruses couldn't  simply jump into humans. Before making that leap,

01:58 they were thought to need months, years, or even  decades of evolution inside animal populations.

02:03 It was like a key that still needed to be  filed down before it could fit the unique

02:07 ‘lock’ of the human body. And that mattered.

02:10 It suggested there was distance between us and the  world's most dangerous viruses.The species barrier

02:16 wasn't just a scientific concept. It became a kind of safety net.

02:20 A belief that we’d have a window to  spot a virus spreading through animal

02:23 populations. To track how it was changing  and stop it before it ever reached up.

02:28 But what if that window never existed? What if the virus was already

02:32 loaded and ready to fire? Recent research reveals that the evolutionary

02:36 barrier model may not be anywhere near as concrete  as we thought. Because if viruses need to mutate

02:41 to infect us, then how did the deadliest  outbreaks in history skip this step entirely?

02:47 To understand the implications

02:48 of this biosecurity blind spot, we have  to go back to one of the worst pandemics

02:53 the Earth has ever seen: the Spanish Flu. In just 2 years, it infected roughly a third

02:57 of the world's population and killed tens of  millions of people. It was a uniquely deadly

03:02 strain of H1N1 influenza and it unleashed  chaos on a scale the world had never seen.

03:08 In the decades that followed, scientists  worked to understand exactly how it happened.

03:12 They traced its path and developed  a model for how pandemics spread.

03:16 For nearly a century, we  thought that model was correct.

03:19 The pandemic was portrayed as a slow-motion  disaster. A chain of events that unfolded over

03:24 years, not months. If there had been a warning  window, the tragedy could have been avoided.

03:29 But that narrative was shattered  around the turn of the millennium.

03:32 Scientists exhumed and analyzed the bodies of  Spanish Flu victims from an Inuit community

03:37 in Brevig Mission, Alaska. The bodies had  been perfectly preserved in the permafrost,

03:42 allowing the researchers to extract samples  of the viral RNA. They were then able to

03:46 effectively reconstruct the virus using  modern genomic sequencing techniques.

03:50 That’s when they uncovered the truth. A truth that rewrote the rulebook

03:54 on how viruses operated. It turned out that the 1918

03:58 H1N1 virus hadn’t spent years mutating in pigs  before making the leap into human populations.

04:04 It was believed to have started as an avian  virus, originating in birds. And somewhere

04:08 along the way, it developed something important:  a ‘human-ready’ Hemagglutinin (HA) protein that

04:14 was already capable of binding to human cells. In other words, the virus already had the ‘key’

04:20 it needed to unlock the doors of the human body. At the very moment of spillover as it passed from

04:25 wild bird populations into humans, it didn’t  need to undergo any sort of rapid mutation.

04:30 It didn’t need to multiply to develop the  tools it needed to launch a global pandemic.

04:35 It was a ‘plug and play’  biological weapon found in nature.

04:38 And that completely defied  everything the scientific

04:41 community had believed about this virus. It called into question the idea of a long

04:45 warning window and the so-called  evolutionary barrier itself.

04:49 But every virus is different. They  mutate and move in different ways.

04:52 With that in mind, scientists were  left with one crucial question:

04:56 was 1918 just a bizarre historical fluke?  A once-in-a-lifetime example of a virus

05:01 breaking convention or is nature mass-producing  these ‘plug and play’ weapons as we speak?

05:06 In 2021, a team of researchers

05:08 discovered something that shattered everything  we believed about how viruses operate.

05:12 It was at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic,  caused by the SARS‑CoV‑2 strain of coronavirus.

05:18 There were a lot of different theories  about how that particular virus began and

05:22 crossed from animals into humans. Several  studies pointed toward bat populations.

05:27 So, the researchers set out to see if  they could find that ‘missing link’.

05:30 They explored the limestone  caves of Laos in Southeast Asia,

05:33 collecting samples from various bat species  and taking them back to the lab for analysis.

05:38 They uncovered a group of wild bat coronaviruses.  Three in particular - named BANAL-52, BANAL-103,

05:45 and BANAL-236 - stood out due to their  distinctive genomic similarities to SARS-CoV-2.

05:51 Further analysis showed that all 3  of them had a specific spike protein

05:55 that was actually able to attach itself  to the ACE2 receptors of human cells.

06:00 ACE2 receptors act like entry points on the  surface of our cells. Think of them as locks

06:05 and the spike protein are the key viruses use  to open them and gain entry into the body.

06:10 All these viruses possessed the necessary key. But that’s not all.

06:14 Using advanced techniques like binding  measurements and computer simulations,

06:18 researchers found something unexpected. The 3  bat viruses behaved almost identically to the

06:23 original Wuhan strain of SARS-CoV-2.  In some cases, they were even better

06:27 at attaching to human cells, giving the body  almost no chance of preventing an infection.

06:32 One of them, BANAL-236, showed clear evidence  of being able to multiply inside human cells.

06:38 These viruses - found far from  urban centers - were, in some ways,

06:42 better equipped to infect humans than the strain  that was, at the same time, shutting down society.

06:48 Then it got worse. Unlike SARS-CoV-2, none of

06:51 the wild viruses possessed a Furin Cleavage Site,  or FCS. This is a unique molecular structure that

06:57 allows viruses to easily fuse with human cells. At the time, COVID-19 skeptics argued that the

07:03 presence of an FCS was proof that SARS-CoV-2  must have been modified in a laboratory. It’s

07:09 such a rare feature in nature. It was the ‘smoking gun,’

07:13 But the wild viruses proved that Mother Nature  was already producing pre-programmed viral

07:18 strains that could, in theory, bypass the  species barrier. Humans could be infected

07:22 far more easily than expected. All without  the slow, step-by-step evolutionary process

07:27 scientists had long assumed was necessary. And if nature is building these human-optimized

07:32 keys in the middle of the jungle,  what happens when they find a lock?

07:36 Middle East respiratory syndrome-related

07:38 coronavirus, otherwise known as MERS-CoV, is  one of the most lethal pathogens on the planet

07:43 This virus causes a condition called MERS, and  can produce a range of symptoms, from fevers and

07:48 coughs to respiratory difficulties and diarrhea. The first case was identified in 2012 in Saudi

07:53 Arabia. Several thousand more have occurred  since then, with an approximately 35% fatality

07:59 rate. There have been several notable outbreaks,  including one in South Korea in 2015, though most

08:05 cases have been isolated to the Arabian Peninsula. Studies have found that humans are typically

08:10 infected with MERS-CoV via contact with camels. If we follow conventional epidemiological models,

08:16 then the virus found in those camels  should be notably different from the

08:19 one found in the cells of dying human  patients. It should show clear evidence

08:24 of countless mutations that enabled it to pass  from one species to the other. The very changes

08:29 that allowed it to survive in the human body. This would confirm the ‘intermediate host’ theory.

08:34 That’s not what the data shows. When researchers used genomic

08:38 sequencing techniques to map out the MERS-CoV  viruses found in both humans and camels,

08:43 they discovered a disturbing fact:  the two are almost exactly the same.

08:48 To be more precise, they’re 99.9% identical. They’re not distant relatives,

08:54 but biological mirror images. That means that this virus doesn’t

08:57 need any sort of learning or adaptation period  to bridge the gap from one species to the other.

09:02 There isn’t some vast chasm separating the  two, but a tiny, almost imperceptible 0.1% gap.

09:09 The virus can simply cross the species barrier,  using the exact same architecture it relies on

09:14 to infect livestock and other animal populations. It’s a fully functional, completely compatible,

09:20 and capable invader. A microscopic  weapon of mass destruction that is

09:24 more adaptable than we ever thought possible. The implications of this are terrifying from a

09:29 biosecurity standpoint. This discovery suggests  that virologists may have been working on flawed

09:34 information for years. They have been looking  for the wrong warning signs, following unreliable

09:40 models, and allowing society to sleepwalk  its way towards another biological crisis.

09:45 If animal-based viruses like MERS-CoV are  already identical to the human-killing versions,

09:50 then how many more of them are out there,  just waiting to kick off the next pandemic?

09:54 By the early 2020s, we knew that

09:56 there were viruses that could move from animals to  humans far faster than anticipated. Scientists had

10:02 proved that this was the case with the  likes of the Spanish Flu and MERS-CoV.

10:06 But they were still seen by  many as outliers or anomalies.

10:09 Then, a groundbreaking 2024 study arrived.  It showed that these alleged anomalies might

10:14 be part of a larger and deeply worrying trend. The study was carried out by researchers at the

10:19 Bloom Lab at the Fred Hutch Cancer Center,  led by evolutionary biologist Jesse Bloom.

10:24 It was designed to put the evolutionary  barrier hypothesis to the ultimate test.

10:29 They wanted to know whether viruses actually  need time to adapt when they jump into humans,

10:34 or whether they might already be  capable of doing it from the start.

10:37 To do this, the team didn’t just focus  on a single outbreak or viral strain.

10:41 Instead, they analyzed large genomic  datasets to understand how they behave

10:46 at a molecular level. They used a technique  called deep mutational scanning to study

10:51 specific viral proteins in detail. Their  analysis covered a wide range of viruses,

10:56 including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, HIV, and Zika. This allowed them to map out how thousands of

11:03 potential mutations might affect a virus’  ability to evade antibodies and infect cells.

11:08 First, the researchers had to create  so-called ‘pseudoviruses’. These were

11:12 safe versions of real pathogens that were able  to enter cells but unable to replicate. This

11:17 eliminated the multiple risks associated with  working with live, dangerous viral strains.

11:22 They were then able to genetically  engineer the viral proteins to make

11:25 their own mutations, exploring. It was similar  to the ways a viral cell might change or adapt

11:30 to increase its infectivity and ability to survive  in different hosts and environments. The variants

11:35 were then tested and researchers measured how  well they resisted antibodies and how tightly

11:40 they attached themselves to host cells. The data pointed in one direction.

11:44 Some of the deadliest pandemics  in human history had zero

11:47 adaptation time during their initial outbreaks. In other words, when these strains first entered

11:53 the human population, they didn’t immediately need  to evolve to become more effective at infecting us

11:58 or evading the immune system. They didn’t need to.

12:01 They were already capable of doing that. This exposes a truly systemic flaw in global

12:07 health surveillance and security. Scientific communities and virology

12:10 initiatives like the USAID PREDICT program  have believed that we should be looking for

12:15 viruses in the wild that are ‘beginning to  evolve’ human-like traits. The ones that

12:20 could pave the way towards widespread infections. Meanwhile, more ‘generalist’ viruses that are able

12:24 to infect multiple species have historically been  viewed as ‘lower-risk’. That’s because they don’t

12:29 appear to be optimized for human transmission. This research has turned those beliefs upside

12:34 down. It suggests that by the time a virus begins  to evolve human traits it is already too late.

12:40 The pandemic has already started.

12:42 Studies seem to suggest that there could be a  number of viruses out there in the wild today,

12:47 just waiting for human hosts to come  along. The one factor that seemed to be

12:51 working in humanity’s favor was that these viral  strains were confined to places far from human

12:56 populations. They appeared to exist primarily  in jungles, caves, and other remote ecosystems.

13:01 If that was true, then it explained  why global pandemics had seemingly

13:05 been once-in-a-century events. People simply  weren’t coming into contact with these viruses.

13:10 The evolutionary barrier model may have been  shattered, but a new ‘geographic barrier’ seemed

13:15 to have emerged. The actual physical distance  between human populations and infected animals

13:20 helps us to stay relatively safe. That was the theory.

13:24 Researchers made yet another frightening discovery  which sent scientific communities back to the

13:29 drawing board to reassess their understanding of  viral biology. They found that people are actually

13:34 encountering these kinds of viruses. All the time.

13:38 A study was carried out involving almost  700 subjects from rural communities in

13:42 Myanmar. They were screened for signs  of sarbecoviruses: specific sorts of

13:47 coronaviruses that mostly infect bats and  have the potential to cross over into humans.

13:52 The study found that 12.1% of the people possessed  antibodies for these viruses. That meant they had

13:58 been exposed to them at some point in the past. People were significantly more likely to test

14:03 positive if they worked in industries that  involved spending time outdoors or handling

14:07 raw materials. This included activities like  logging, hunting, and harvesting forest products.

14:12 It was an important finding. On average, over 1 in 10 people in these parts of

14:17 the world have been infected by wild viruses. Most  of it appears linked to bats, with some evidence

14:23 also pointing to pangolins. But when you check  official public health records from these same

14:28 areas, you won’t find reports of major outbreaks.  There’s no unexpected spikes in atypical

14:33 infections, no sudden lockdowns or quarantines. But the clues are all there.

14:37 They’re hidden in the blood of these individuals. Those clues are the remnants of the silent ‘test

14:42 fires’ of weapons that haven’t  yet been fully triggered.

14:45 The old explanations of how viruses work have  been well and truly obliterated by this stage.

14:51 Humans aren’t as special as we were led to  believe. Not in the eyes of viruses, in any case.

14:55 We’re just the next step in the chain. Viruses  already have everything they need to infect us,

15:00 and they’re actively doing so, albeit in  places that don’t dominate the headlines.

15:05 If everything we’ve seen so far is accurate,  then humanity’s days must be numbered.

15:10 Evidence suggests that mankind has been

15:12 lucky to survive this far with so many  potentially deadly viruses circulating

15:16 in nature. Fortunately, there’s one thing that  has been working in our favor, this entire time.

15:22 Our last line of defense. A biological safeguard that

15:25 has helped keep humanity alive for generations.  One that has allowed us to survive pandemics

15:30 that killed tens of millions. It’s called the Interferon response.

15:34 And it acts like the body’s built-in firewall. When a human-ready virus enters the body,

15:38 the data suggests it has no trouble binding to  receptors and entering cells. It already carries

15:43 the key it needs to unlock those biological locks.  That’s the easy part. Because the moment it enters

15:49 the body, something else begins. An invisible countdown.

15:52 If the virus doesn’t move fast enough, it won’t  have the freedom it needs to replicate and spread.

15:57 Instead, it’ll be killed out in a matter of hours. This is where the Interferon response comes in.

16:02 Interferons are a group of signaling proteins,  also known as cytokines. They’re produced by

16:08 the body in response to the presence of foreign  microbes, like viruses and bacteria. As their name

16:13 suggests, Interferons are designed to interfere  with these invaders. They slow them down,

16:18 disrupt their replication, and make it  harder for them to take hold in the body.

16:22 They do this in various ways, including  actively degrading viral RNA and alerting

16:27 other cells to defend themselves against the  coming threat. Studies show that the majority

16:31 of wild viruses are entirely neutralized  by this initial cellular counter-attack.

16:36 Even though the viruses have the key to pass the  front door, they soon discover that the house is

16:41 equipped with a state of the art security system. Because for viruses, the real challenge isn’t

16:45 just getting inside the body or even entering  cells. It’s surviving long enough to replicate.

16:51 To multiply fast enough to gain control  before the immune system shuts them down.

16:56 This is the only thing that’s saving us from  a perpetual state of pandemic emergency.

17:01 The warning window depends on the virus itself.  Some viruses mutate quickly, allowing them to

17:05 weaken or evade interferon responses. Others are  stopped earlier. It also depends on the body’s own

17:11 ability to detect the invasion fast enough. To sound the alarm.

17:15 And activate its defenses  before the virus can spread.

17:18 This is why those 1 in 10 people in the rural  villages of Myanmar have those antibodies.

17:22 Yes, their systems were invaded by wild  viruses from bats and other creatures,

17:27 but it didn’t trigger a massive outbreak or  society-halting pandemic. Their bodies were able

17:32 to respond in time and their Interferons  did the job they were designed to do.

17:36 The enemy was effectively eliminated  just inside the castle gates.

17:40 But why is nature building these  human-ready keys in the first place

17:43 if we aren’t the primary target?

17:45 It’s clear humanity has been following  a fundamental misunderstanding

17:49 of viral evolution for generations. We have spent decades believing that viruses

17:53 have to adapt to us because we’re so different and  distinct compared to other animals. Humanity has

17:59 represented the ultimate prize for these microbes,  the pinnacle of their evolutionary pathways.

18:04 The data tells a very different story. It shows that the most successful viral

18:08 strains in history - like the 1918 Spanish Flu  and SARS-CoV-2 COVID-19 - didn’t show any major

18:15 signs of recent human adaptation. These were what virologists

18:18 refer to as ‘generalist’ viruses. They didn’t evolve in the wilderness or mutate

18:23 in dense jungles. They weren’t pre-programmed to  infect and kill humans specifically. They didn’t

18:28 even require years of random mutations  to reach their ‘human-ready’ forms.

18:32 They simply evolved over time to survive in  high-density, multi-species environments.

18:36 They learned to thrive in places where bats,  birds, rodents, primates, and other creatures were

18:41 present. That gives them an enormous advantage. viruses spread more easily when they aren’t

18:46 limited to a single species. These viruses  effectively come with their very own skeleton keys

18:51 that allow them to go almost anywhere they please.  In other words, people aren’t the targets. They’re

18:56 not the end goals or ultimate objectives. They’re just collateral damage.

19:00 This is what makes the next  pandemic an invisible inevitability.

19:04 The hardware is already there. And it’s fully compatible

19:06 with the human operating system. When nature is creating its own biological

19:10 weapons, humanity isn’t sitting on the sidelines.  And when things go wrong, it has consequences.

19:16 Discover the horrifying truth in “Viruses That  Were Actually Lab Leaks”. Or watch this video.

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 The archives are open. In its history  of over a hundred years, the FBI has

00:03 classified many documents - until now. Now, these  government secrets are open for anyone to see.

00:09 Here are fifty of the most  insane declassified secrets

00:12 of the FBI - including details on one  of America’s most mysterious residents.

00:17 #50. Alive or Dead?

00:19 In the aftermath of World War II, the entire world  celebrated the death of the Nazi leader Adolf

00:24 Hitler. But despite the confirmation that his life  had ended in a Berlin bunker as the Allied troops

00:29 marched in, rumors started to spread. Did Hitler  actually escape like so many of his Nazi allies,

00:35 maybe to South America? Did he shave his mustache  and go undercover as an everyday suburban man,

00:40 as one ill-advised sitcom imagined? The rumors  persisted enough that in the months after the war,

00:45 the FBI investigated evidence of his survival. And  the declassified documents showed…nope, he’s dead.

00:51 It wasn’t the only FBI  investigation related to the war.

00:54 #49. The Wife

00:56 J. Robert Oppenheimer, the brilliant physicist  heavily responsible for the United States

01:00 winning the race to the atom bomb, was largely  trusted by the US government despite some past

01:05 leftist ties. But he was also married -  and the FBI had some doubts about her.

01:10 A trained biologist, she worked for the government  at Los Alamos to help determine the body’s

01:15 vulnerability to radiation. The FBI was more  concerned with her early life, when she had been

01:19 involved with communist activist Joseph Dallet Jr.  and joined the Communist Party. This led to her

01:24 being investigated by agents about current ties,  and to her husband’s clearance being reduced.

01:29 But many FBI investigations during  the era were much more wide-reaching.

01:34 #48. Detention!

01:35 Even before President Roosevelt’s infamous  executive order that led to the imprisonment of

01:40 the United States’ Japanese-American population,  the government was hard at work arresting people.

01:45 During the war, anyone deemed a security threat  could be rounded up and detained by the government

01:49 during the national state of emergency - and it  centered on three groups. Japanese-Americans,

01:54 German-Americans, and Italian-Americans were  all arrested with little room for appeal,

01:59 and the FBI kept an exhaustive  list of the numbers.

02:02 But being investigated by the  FBI isn’t always a negative.

02:05 #47. The Money Man

02:07 It’s rare for someone to play a key role in the  home front in two world wars, but Bernard Baruch

02:12 wasn’t an ordinary man. The stock market magnate  was chairman of the War Industries Board under

02:17 Woodrow Wilson, and advised President Roosevelt  on industry and production decades later.

02:22 When anyone is that close to the President,  the FBI will want to take a look at him.

02:25 Did they find any red flags on the man?  Given that he was later appointed to the

02:29 United Nations Atomic Energy Commission  by Harry Truman, that’s likely a no.

02:33 And in some cases, it’s about  confirming what’s already known.

02:36 #46. Operation Paperclip

02:39 When the US government decided to recruit  former Nazis to help with the nuclear and

02:42 space programs after the war, they knew they  would need thorough background checks. After all,

02:47 they were okay with some Nazis, but not  the worst of the worst. The FBI was tasked

02:51 with digging into the wartime activities of  these scientists and deciding if they were

02:54 valuable and relatively clean enough to become  Americans. Now on the FBI’s websites, Americans

03:00 can dig into the original reports of figures  like Arthur Randolph and Wernher Von Braun.

03:04 But sometimes, the FBI was looking  to prevent war before it happened.

03:08 #45. Flying SOLO

03:10 While the US never went to  war with the Soviet Union,

03:13 paranoia was high about the communist nation  infiltrating and sabotaging the Americans.

03:18 That’s why the FBI created SOLO, an intelligence  effort that spanned two decades. It placed agents

03:23 within the Communist Party of the United States  to discover if they were passing information

03:27 to communist nations like the Soviet Union  or China. The operation was largely headed

03:31 by two agents - now declassified as Russian  Jewish immigrants Morris and Jack Childs,

03:36 whose background gave them the skills needed  to infiltrate Russian communist enclaves.

03:40 But not every espionage  investigation is above board.

03:44 #44. In the Bag

03:45 How do you get a search warrant when the  subject of the investigation is classified?

03:49 Simple - you don’t. During the 1940s and  beyond, the FBI frequently pulled off what

03:53 was called Black Bag Operations. This was when the  organization would simply break into residences or

03:59 businesses under the cover of darkness and search  for evidence, without ever informing the subject

04:03 of the search that they were being watched. Many  of these never escalated to criminal prosecutions,

04:08 so they weren’t disclosed until the files  were declassified. The tactic continued

04:12 until 1966 when the bureau ordered it stopped,  and it was declared unconstitutional in 1972.

04:18 But not all targets of FBI  investigation are as obvious.

04:22 #43. The Lady of Peace

04:24 Jane Addams was one of the most  prominent early feminist reformers,

04:27 a tireless advocate in the progressive era  for women’s suffrage and public housing.

04:31 She even became the first American woman to be  awarded with the Nobel Peace Prize for her role

04:35 in the anti-war and anti-imperialist movement.  So why is there an FBI file on this woman?

04:40 How about a treason investigation? When World War  I began, Addams held fast to her anti-war beliefs

04:46 and she founded a women’s party devoted to peace.  In the 1920s, when she opposed the persecution of

04:51 communist activists, the FBI started monitoring  her - but came up empty on criminal charges.

04:56 But one peace movement led to more  investigations than any other.

05:00 #42. Yippie?

05:02 The Vietnam War was deeply controversial,  and many anti-war activists wound up being

05:06 investigated by the government.  Chief among them was Abbie Hoffman,

05:10 whose brushes with the law would lead to what  became known as “The Trial of the Chicago Eight”.

05:14 His group, the Youth International  Party, better known as the Yippies,

05:18 was frequently investigated by the FBI over a  period of five years. Those digging through the

05:22 FBI archives will find a whopping fifty-part  series on the colorful figure - who wound up

05:27 being portrayed by Sacha Baron Cohen in  the movie The Trial of the Chicago 7.

05:31 One bloody day would come to define the Vietnam

05:33 protest movement and lead to  years of FBI investigation.

05:37 #41. Blood on American Soil

05:40 It started out as any other peace rally in  1970, with students at Kent State University

05:44 in Ohio protesting the National Guard presence  on campus as the war expanded to Cambodia.

05:49 But what wasn’t typical was the National  Guard opening fire on the unarmed crowd,

05:54 killing four students and wounding nine others.  Two of the dead were bystanders, not protestors,

05:59 and massive rallies around the country  protested the killings. Ultimately,

06:02 none of the Guardsmen who fired were criminally  prosecuted, but the FBI spent years investigating

06:07 the shooting - and all those documents can  now be read in a twenty-two part series.

06:11 But some FBI cases are a lot less serious.

06:15 #40. There’s No Place Like Home?

06:17 Few pieces of movie memorabilia are more iconic-  Dorothy’s iconic ruby slippers from The Wizard

06:23 of Oz. That’s why it was such big news when they  were stolen from the Judy Garland Museum in 2005.

06:28 This theft was reported to the police, but the  interstate smuggling operation was soon taken over

06:32 by the FBI. It took the government organization  more than ten years to track down the thief,

06:37 and even then it took multiple agents  on a sting operation before the rare

06:41 shoes were returned back home where they belonged.

06:43 But some cases may be a little silly.

06:46 #39. Sing That Song

06:48 “Louie Louie, oh no. Me gotta go”. The  song’s probably stuck in your head now,

06:54 right? But what does it actually mean? No  one really knows - and neither did the FBI.

06:59 When the popular song by The Kingsmen debuted  in 1963, it became a sensation, and many people

07:04 wondered if the song was hiding a dirty little  secret. Were the words secretly pornographic? Were

07:09 they hiding a coded political message? The FBI  spent a full year investigating the song and its

07:13 creators - and came up empty, as the lyrics remain  as unintelligible as they were back in 1963.

07:19 It wasn’t the only time the  FBI got involved in music.

07:22 #38. Not Fab

07:25 Everyone loved the Beatles - if their  army of screaming fans was any indication.

07:29 But the government wasn’t as fond of the  shaggy-haired British band, and the Nixon

07:33 administration had a particular grudge against  left-wing songwriter John Lennon. Nixon was

07:38 convinced that Lennon was plotting to influence  the 1972 election with his popularity, and the

07:42 FBI launched an investigation that led to the  Immigration and Naturalization Service starting

07:47 the process of deporting Lennon. While Lennon was  never banned from the country, he did back off

07:52 plans for an American tour - a victory for Nixon  that was later exposed by journalist Jon Weiner.

07:57 But you might be shocked by just  how many celebrities have FBI files.

08:02 #37. Before the White House

08:04 Ronald Reagan having an FBI file  shouldn’t be a surprise - after all,

08:08 they probably like to know about the  President. But he was on the agency’s

08:11 radar long before 1980. In 1947, when he  was President of the Screen Actors Guild,

08:16 he had a file - but why would they want  to know about the staunch conservative,

08:20 surely the last suspect anyone would have as  a communist agent? Because Reagan was such a

08:25 strong anti-communist that he and his then-wife  Jane Wyman worked with federal agents to turn

08:30 over the name of actors they thought might be  communists. The future President was an informant.

08:35 But one more beloved figure had FBI ties as well.

08:38 #36. The Mouse’s Secret

08:40 Walt Disney was notorious  for being a traditionalist,

08:43 and the man behind Mickey Mouse and the Disney  parks didn’t like anything that shattered

08:47 the illusion of all-American happiness in his  properties. That included people with unpopular

08:51 political views which led to his deep ties  with the government. He had worked with them

08:55 on World War II propaganda films, and long  after the war he was still cooperating with

09:00 them - giving them information on un-American  activities in Hollywood. He continued working

09:04 with them through his death in 1966, and was even  named a full Special Agent in Charge Contact.

09:10 But many celebrities have files  for less official reasons.

09:14 #35. The Lady Sings

09:16 Why would Whitney Houston have an FBI file?  The late singer lived a controversial life,

09:21 and it got her on the government’s radar.  While her troubles with drugs and money and

09:24 her often chaotic relationships landed her in  the tabloids, the FBI was more interested in

09:29 her associates. Many people from her  life tried to take advantage of her,

09:32 including a stalker who tried to blackmail  her for a quarter of a million dollars.

09:36 But why would one of the least-controversial  singers of all time be on the list?

09:41 #34. Take Me Home?

09:43 John Denver seemed like the guy next door, with  his easy-listening country music songs being

09:47 the type your parents sing along to on a long  car ride. But the FBI saw things differently.

09:52 Up until his death in a plane crash, Denver  had amassed a thirty-three-page FBI file.

09:56 It was mostly concerned with his anti-war activism  as a young man and his occasional drug use,

10:01 but it also followed stalkers and death  threats he picked up as a celebrity.

10:05 The FBI even got involved in  some notorious tabloid stories.

10:09 #33. The Bombshell

10:11 Anna Nicole Smith was famous for marrying  a much older man - who died not long after.

10:16 She inherited most of his fortune, much to the  anger of the oil tycoon’s son E. Pierce Marshall.

10:21 The two were involved in a vicious  court battle over the massive bank

10:24 account - vicious enough for Marshall to  believe Smith tried to kill him. This led

10:28 to an FBI investigation that ultimately decided  there wasn’t enough to charge Smith. Ultimately,

10:33 it was all for nothing - Marshall and Smith died  within a year of each other in 2006 and 2007.

10:39 But even the original bombshell  was on the FBI’s radar.

10:42 #32. Government Prefers Blondes?

10:45 Marilyn Monroe has been the subject  of countless government conspiracies

10:49 due to her mysterious death. But the FBI wasn’t  interested in that - they were more concerned

10:53 with her love life. One of Monroe’s many  loves was acclaimed playwright Arthur Miller,

10:58 who was believed to have Communist leanings.  Due to Monroe’s influence, the FBI kept an

11:02 eye on her - which led many to believe the  government might have been involved in her death.

11:06 She wasn’t the only icon to  wind up in the FBI’s files.

11:10 #31. Loooooooocy!

11:12 Everyone loved Lucille Ball, who along with  husband Desi Arnaz created one of the most

11:17 iconic sitcoms of all time. But Ball was an  eccentric woman, who once claimed she picked

11:22 up spy chatter with her tooth fillings. The FBI  was more concerned with her political leanings,

11:26 as the comedy star had been affiliated with  the communist party in the 1930s. Ball was

11:30 repeatedly interviewed and denied having any  ongoing communist affiliations. While she was

11:35 never placed on the notorious blacklists  of the 1950s, her file grew to 156 pages.

11:40 But some stars had a rougher road with the FBI.

11:43 #30. Hardly Silent

11:45 Charlie Chaplin was best known for physical  comedy and for famously opposing Hitler with

11:49 his silent film The Great Dictator.  But he was anything but silent off

11:53 the screen - he was a political activist who  was believed to be a communist sympathizer.

11:58 Chaplin was a British citizen who worked a lot in  the United States, and J. Edgar Hoover wanted to

12:02 make that more difficult. He even famously blocked  Chaplin’s return to the United States in 1952,

12:08 which led Chaplin and his wife to  depart for Switzerland permanently.

12:11 This next target wasn’t afraid to fight back.

12:14 #29. Turnabout is Fair Play

12:17 Truman Capote likely expected to be  investigated by the FBI. After all,

12:21 the author behind Breakfast at Tiffany’s  was a well-known left-wing activist

12:24 who supported Fidel Castro in Cuba and exposed the  injustices of the US justice system. But why did

12:30 the colorful author have a two-hundred-page FBI  file? That might be because he made a personal

12:35 enemy of J. Edgar Hoover by spreading rumors that  the FBI chief was in a homosexual relationship.

12:40 Sometimes, it’s not anything someone does  - it’s what the FBI thinks they can get.

12:46 #28. Hard Rock

12:47 Rock Hudson was one of the first true matinee  idols, a handsome movie star who became a

12:53 sensation in the 1960s. But he had a secret -  and the FBI was ready to take advantage. Hudson,

12:58 a closeted gay man, was interviewed by the FBI  and the thirty-four page FBI file can be accessed

13:04 online - but not all of it. The file is still  heavily redacted, which has led many to wonder

13:09 what the FBI wanted with Hudson, who famously  became one of Hollywood’s first AIDS casualties.

13:14 Sports brought a surprising number  of figures to the FBI’s attention.

13:18 #27. The Breakthrough

13:20 Few figures in American history have become more  universally loved than Jackie Robinson, the man

13:25 who broke Major League Baseball’s color barrier.  But after his accomplishment, Robinson refused to

13:29 be quiet and play ball. He became involved in the  civil rights movement and supported Presidential

13:34 candidates from both parties. But what got  him on the FBI’s radar was his support of a

13:38 Harlem facility for the International Workers  Order, which supposedly had communist ties.

13:43 But one sports icon was on the FBI’s  radar for far less savory reasons.

13:48 #26. Shame of the Yankees

13:50 George Steinbrenner was many things,  including the owner of the Yankees

13:54 during one of their most successful periods.  But he was also a notorious crook. He made

13:58 illegal donations to Nixon’s re-election  campaign, wound up paying a $15,000 fine,

14:03 and then campaigned to be pardoned of the  charges. While he eventually got his wish,

14:07 his shady financial dealings led him to have an  extensive FBI file from 1986 to his death in 2010.

14:14 Sometimes, people get investigated  before a big promotion.

14:17 #25. The Man for the Jobs?

14:20 Steve Jobs is a big name to anyone who  loves their apple computer or iPad,

14:24 but he was on the government’s radar as early  as 1991. George H. W. Bush was considering

14:30 appointing him to the Export Council, and the  FBI conducted routine background checks. What

14:34 they found wasn’t routine, and it likely  torpedoed his appointment. Not only did

14:39 they find out that he experimented with LSD as  a teenager and spoke positively of the drug,

14:43 but many people stated that they believed  Jobs was a serial liar and manipulator.

14:48 But why would the FBI investigate…Helen Keller?

14:51 #24. Silent No More

14:53 Most people know Helen Keller as the young  deaf-blind child who was taught to communicate

14:58 by vision-impaired schoolteacher Anne Sullivan.  But as soon as Keller learned to communicate,

15:02 she was determined to never be silenced  again. She became involved in feminist causes,

15:07 opposed President Wilson’s policies,  and even co-founded the American Civil

15:11 Liberties Union. A proud socialist, she  quickly wound up on the government’s radar,

15:14 where she has a forty-five-page FBI file.  Something she would no doubt be proud of.

15:19 But many of the FBI’s files were  about the infamous, not the famous.

15:23 #23. The Big Man

15:25 Few names appear in the FBI’s archives more than  Al Capone, the legendary Prohibition-era gangster.

15:31 While Al Capone’s most storied opponent was  Agent Eliot Ness, Ness never worked for the

15:36 FBI - but the bureau was keeping tabs on  him anyway. Capone was ultimately tripped

15:40 up not by his smuggling and mob activities,  but because he underpaid the government

15:44 and was nabbed for tax evasion - something  the FBI’s 36 files on him no doubt caught.

15:49 Even Supreme Court Justices  could be on the bureau’s radar.

15:53 #22. The Good Judge

15:55 Thurgood Marshall had a complex  life, rising from being a civil

15:58 rights activist and lawyer to becoming the  first Black judge on the Supreme Court.

16:02 But his FBI file doesn’t look the same as most  activists. As an early member of the NAACP,

16:08 Marshall knew that he would be spied on.  That’s why the savvy scholar reached out to

16:12 J. Edgar Hoover in the 1950s and met with FBI  leadership. By providing information to them,

16:16 he helped to protect the organization from  accusations of being a communist front.

16:20 But not all judges had such a stellar reputation.

16:24 #21. The Bad Judge?

16:26 When Abe Fortas was appointed to the Supreme Court  by Lyndon Johnson in 1965, he was already a close

16:32 ally of the President - maybe too close. He was  plagued by rumors of obstruction of justice,

16:36 and when he was going to be elevated to  Chief Justice after only three years,

16:40 the investigation picked up heat. The FBI files  even showed that he had been the target of serious

16:45 threats. Ultimately, his nomination for Chief  Justice failed and Fortas resigned from the court.

16:50 And some cases are more by public demand.

16:53 #20. Where Did She Go?

16:55 When Amelia Earhart disappeared during her  attempt to be the first woman to fly across

16:58 the Atlantic ocean, it was highly unlikely  to be a criminal case. Everyone believed

17:03 that she had encountered some mechanical  or weather trouble and likely crashed,

17:06 never to be seen again. But that didn’t stop the  iconic airwoman’s 1937 disappearance from being

17:12 looked into. Countless Americans wrote in to the  FBI asking for assistance in finding her - and

17:17 while there was never an investigation,  her file mostly consists of those letters.

17:21 It wasn’t the only disaster  to get an FBI investigation.

17:24 #19. Up in Smoke

17:26 The Hindenburg zeppelin disaster became one  of the most famous air disasters of all time

17:30 when the massive airship caught fire, killing  thirty-five people. While it’s now considered

17:35 a tragic accident, the FBI initially investigated  it for sabotage. Their case focused on one Joseph

17:41 Spah, a comic acrobat who was one of the first  passengers to see signs of trouble and jumped

17:47 before the ship crashed, suffering only minor  injuries. While Spah was seen as an anti-Nazi

17:52 activist and accused of being a saboteur, the FBI  didn’t find any evidence of an organized plot.

17:58 Another, even more famous disaster  wound up on the FBI’s radar.

18:02 #18. The Challenge

18:03 When the Space Shuttle Challenger went up in  flames, taking all its astronauts with it,

18:07 the cold war was still at its peak  and paranoia was running high.

18:11 Could the Soviet Union have struck a  devastating blow against the US space program?

18:15 The FBI investigated, with over a hundred  pages of reports now declassified - and

18:19 much like the Hindenburg, didn’t come up  with any evidence of sabotage or terrorism.

18:24 Sometimes, the FBI gets closer to  Hollywood than you might expect

18:27 #17. Reel Life

18:29 Why would the FBI have files on a noir film from  1951? Because the title was “I Was a Communist

18:35 for the FBI” and it followed the story of a  real spy who worked for the FBI in the 1940s.

18:41 The film was a patriotic thriller  that portrayed the Second Red Scare

18:44 as a justified response to the threat of Communism  - but the FBI still had to investigate to make

18:49 sure they were being portrayed well and  no classified documents were being leaked.

18:53 But not every FBI file is serious business.

18:56 #16. Thumbs Up

18:58 Why would Gene Siskel, the late film critic  best known for sparring with Roger Ebert

19:02 on which film deserved a thumbs-up, be in the  FBI’s files? Was someone there a really big fan

19:07 of The Silence of the Lambs, which he memorably  panned? Siskel’s FBI file is one of the shortest,

19:13 only one page - a letter from FBI Director William  Sessions congratulating him on winning the Golden

19:18 Plate Award. Receiving that letter from the FBI  was probably terrifying before it was opened.

19:22 It wasn’t the only time the FBI got involved  in things that might be considered silly.

19:27 #15. Hollyweird

19:29 While Lucille Ball was investigated on her own,  it isn’t the only time her sitcom showed up in

19:33 the FBI files. In 1977, the FBI was pulled into  an elaborate copyright infringement scheme when

19:38 they were tipped off by studios that someone  was attempting to illegally distribute copies

19:43 of famous movies and TV shows. In addition to  Lucy, these included classics like The Partridge

19:47 Family and The Twilight Zone. Not exactly high  crimes - but the studios thought differently.

19:52 But not every file the FBI has  declassified is a case file.

19:56 #14. So YOU Want to Be an FBI Agent

19:59 If you want to wear the badge, you’d better start  studying. The FBI doesn’t take just anyone - and

20:04 the best information you might get comes from the  agency themselves. The legal handbook for special

20:09 agents was released as part of the FBI archives,  containing a hundred and thirty-seven pages of the

20:13 procedures they use to track the bad guys. Just  don’t count on it teaching you everything - the

20:18 version released is almost twenty years  old, at the very dawn of the digital era.

20:22 And you might be surprised by who  you find in the FBI’s archives.

20:25 #13. My Privacy!

20:27 Digging through the archives, you’ll find both  famous names and non-famous ones who got on the

20:31 FBI’s radar. They can spy on just about anyone  if they have cause, and most of their targets

20:36 don’t get charged and never find out they were  investigated. That means they could have files

20:40 on everyone - even you. If you’re feeling  paranoid all of a sudden, the good news is,

20:44 you can find out. A Freedom of Information Act  request can unseal those files on you if they

20:49 exist and aren’t classified - if you’re ready  to see their thoughts on your browsing history.

20:54 But some FBI cases are just  bizarre. Look to the skies…

20:58 #12. The First Memo

21:00 Guy Hottel was a special agent working at  the Washington Field Office who seemed to

21:04 be a competent man, which made it all  the more surprising when he sent a

21:07 bizarre memo in March 1950. He claimed  to be relaying information from an Air

21:11 Force investigator about the recovery  of three flying saucers in New Mexico.

21:15 Not only did he describe them in detail,  but the memo claimed that three bodies of

21:19 extraterrestrials were recovered. Needless to  say, no evidence of this was ever confirmed.

21:24 But it wouldn’t be the only  investigation into UFOs by the FBI.

21:28 #11. The Con Man

21:30 Silas M. Newton was already a powerful man in  the oil industry when he contacted the FBI.

21:34 He claimed to have a device that could  find minerals and oil in the ground,

21:37 and was generally regarded as a charlatan.  That didn’t stop him from claiming he had seen

21:41 a flying saucer crash-land on his territory  in 1950. No evidence of it was ever found,

21:47 and he later changed his story. The FBI’s  six-part file on him covers almost twenty

21:51 years of con artist tactics, but it hasn’t  stopped UFO fans from using him as a source.

21:56 But was the FBI really concealing the truth?

21:59 #10. Not So Majestic

22:01 It was one of the biggest bombshells in  the search for UFOs - a document titled

22:05 “Operation Majestic 12”. Sent  to two different FBI offices,

22:09 it revealed a conspiracy dating back  to the Eisenhower administration

22:12 to recover and investigate alien spacecraft and  conceal it from the public. The twenty-two-page

22:17 memo would have been the biggest scandal  in government history - if it was real.

22:22 An investigation revealed it to be a forgery, and  it was uploaded with one additional word - BOGUS.

22:27 But some famous UFOs were investigated.

22:30 #9. What Happened at Roswell?

22:32 For over seventy years, the events in Roswell,  New Mexico have fascinated the public.

22:36 And while it’s been exaggerated in many  ways, there was a real event - and a

22:40 one-page FBI memo describes it. People  reported a mysterious flying disc,

22:45 shaped like a hexagon and suspended from a  balloon. Not exactly the massive alien spacecraft,

22:50 with many people thinking it resembled an  odd weather balloon more than an invasion.

22:54 One particularly terrifying  phenomenon wound up on their radar.

22:57 #8. Those Poor Cows

23:00 In the 1970s, western and prairie states  found themselves dealing with a rash of

23:04 animal mutilations, mainly cattle. The  animals often had odd sigils carved into

23:08 them and seemed like they had been mauled by  some sort of machine - at least that’s what

23:12 the descriptions said. While many possible  causes that weren’t alien were proposed,

23:16 including satanic cults, no answer to  the disturbing phenomenon was ever found.

23:21 It was enough to get the organization  to actually start a new division.

23:24 #7. Look to the Skies

23:27 There were enough reports of strange sights in  the sky that a new organization was founded,

23:31 the National Investigations Committee on Aerial  Phenomena. Starting in the 1950s, it worked with

23:36 the FBI to share reports of unexplained flying  objects and determine possible causes. While the

23:41 correspondence didn’t actually result in any  UFOs being discovered, the bureau continued

23:46 working with them as well as cooperating with the  Air Force on a project titled Project Blue Book.

23:51 But did the FBI ever crack the code of  the country’s most notorious location?

23:55 #6. Let’s Break In!

23:57 Sure, a bunch of guys on the internet thought  they could break into Area 51 and free ET,

24:01 but we’re no closer to figuring out exactly what’s  in there. Does the FBI archive help with that? Not

24:06 really - Area 51 isn’t under their jurisdiction,  and most people working there might not even know.

24:11 To get some clues, you’d have to look at their  rival agency the CIA, which did actually mention

24:16 Area 51 in some documents - with no details,  and no hints about what might be inside.

24:21 But the FBI did investigate  some seriously bizarre thing.

24:24 #5. Mind-Readers

24:26 Is ESP a real phenomenon? Are there actually  people who can read minds or predict things

24:31 before they happen? The FBI vault states  that ESP is considered a perception of

24:35 information about events beyond what can be  learned from the senses or past knowledge.

24:40 It’s a vague phenomenon, and the investigation  didn’t make it any clearer - they spent three

24:44 years and likely a lot of money to determine  there was no scientific support for ESP.

24:49 And sometimes, the FBI might  be its own worst enemy.

24:52 #4. The Rivalry

24:54 The FBI handles domestic affairs and  the CIA handles international affairs.

24:58 You’d think that would make them natural allies  - but it doesn’t always work out that way.

25:02 The two agencies can be bitter rivals and  hesitant to share information. That often

25:06 leads to missed opportunities for cooperation,  especially in cases where international threats

25:11 are plotting against the United States  homeland - like what happened on 9/11.

25:15 And what does the FBI say about that fateful day?

25:18 #3. The 9/11 Files

25:20 Few files were more anticipated  for declassification than the first

25:23 documents on the September 11th, 2001 attacks.  Particularly, many people were wondering if it

25:28 would shed light on possible involvement by the  Saudi Royal Family in the attacks - and other

25:33 conspiracy theorists wondered if it would  reveal that the US government was involved.

25:37 The documents shed some light on intelligence  failures, but didn’t implicate anyone new.

25:41 Sometimes, Hollywood doesn’t live up to the hype.

25:44 #2. Declassified?

25:46 When CBS announced a new documentary series  titled “The FBI Declassified” in 2020,

25:51 many people wondered how they could get  away with this. Were they sharing government

25:55 secrets? Would the FBI break the door down  mid-broadcast? It turned out the answer was…no

25:59 on all counts. The six-episode documentary  shared profiles on some well-known cases,

26:04 but didn’t declassify anything - which  probably accounted for the low ratings.

26:08 But one case might be more  mysterious than any other.

26:12 #1. Getting Hairy

26:13 There is no American legend that  fascinates people more than Bigfoot.

26:18 Is there really a giant, hairy humanoid lurking  in the woods? The rumors were enough that the

26:22 FBI actually investigated the legend in the  1970s, combing the woods for evidence of hairs,

26:27 footprints, and waste material. In 1976,  they actually did find long hairs that

26:32 couldn’t be matched to any species. The  declassified investigation was declared

26:36 inconclusive - which was more than enough for  true believers to say the truth is out there.

26:41 For more on the government’s secrets, check  out “10 Craziest CIA Covert Operations”,

26:46 or watch this video instead.

docs.text:
00:00 What’s the last thing that goes through your mind  when you’re shot in the head? Well… apart from the

00:04 bullet. We’re breaking down what happens in those  final moments - how the brain reacts, what you

00:09 might feel and why Hollywood gets it wrong.This is  what really happens when you’re shot in the head.

00:11 Ok, staring down the business end of a loaded  gun is hardly an everyday situation for many

00:12 of us. Even those who find themselves drawn  to more ‘armed and dangerous’ lines of work

00:12 are statistically unlikely to see a gun fight,  let alone be part of one. But the chances are,

00:12 if there’s a gun pointed at your head,  the person holding it might be reckless

00:12 – or desperate – enough to pull that trigger. Let’s say you’re standing just a few feet from

00:14 someone with a gun pointed squarely at your head.  Maybe it’s a mob hitman. Maybe a bitter ex. Or

00:20 maybe just a violent psychopath who left their  tinfoil hat at home. The reason doesn’t matter.

00:25 What does matter is that their aim  is solid. Their range is close. And

00:29 there's no chance they’re going to miss. The second that the trigger is squeezed,

00:33 before the bullet has even left the gun and  entered your soft squishy brain, there’s already a

00:38 whole lot going on. Inside the chamber of that gun  sits a cartridge – what most people wrongly call a

00:43 bullet. The bullet is the projectile at the tip  - the rest is the cartridge casing, packed with

00:48 propellant and sealed with a primer at the base. So, the gun is loaded and cocked. The firing pin

00:54 is held back under spring tension, resting  right behind the cartridge. And now - with

00:58 one final pull - it’s released. The firing pin  snaps forward, punching the primer at the base

01:03 of the cartridge. That tiny impact causes a spark,  igniting the chemical powder inside and creating

01:09 an instant explosion within the cartridge.  The propellant chemicals burn and generate

01:14 a lot of expanding gas, very quickly, causing a  massive build up of pressure. Being bottled up in

01:20 such a small place means there’s only really  one direction all that pressure can travel:

01:25 outwards. And bullet cartridges are  designed to channel the pressure

01:29 from that mini explosion – and all the kinetic  energy it causes – directly behind the bullet.

01:35 The bullet splits off from the end of the  cartridge, and is sent down the barrel at high

01:38 speeds. Most bullets are tapered into a point,  which both helps to reduce air resistance as they

01:43 come speeding out of a weapon. But that tapered  tip is also helpful for allowing the projectile to

01:48 penetrate wood, metal, or in this case, your head. Now, it’s important to bear in mind, everything

01:53 we’ve described so far has all occurred within  only a few seconds – it’s so fast that your

01:57 brain likely hasn’t even had a chance to  process half of what’s happened. And even

02:01 more unfortunately for you, that’s not the only  problem that your brain is going to have today.

02:05 Whenever we see gunshots on TV, in movies or even  inflict them on other players in video games,

02:11 deaths often seem to happen instantaneously.  Sometimes you might see a character struck by

02:16 a bullet and suffering a slow and painful  death and sometimes characters will shrug

02:20 off bullet wounds no problem. In real life, these  are all possible: instant death, a slow, agonising

02:26 fatal injury or surviving - although this is in  extremely rare cases. But it all comes down to a

02:32 myriad of factors, and while you might think that  a head shot is the fast track to our first instant

02:37 death option, you’d be surprised – and we’ve  found a real world example to prove that too.

02:43 First among these factors is all down to the  specifics; what type of firearm was used,

02:48 what size and calibre are the bullets it’s  firing. Then there’s the trajectory the bullet

02:52 was travelling and what angle it entered your  body. All of these might seem like small details,

02:57 but they can all mean the difference between life,  death and something arguably worse. That’s because

03:02 being shot, well, it’s all a matter of physics! Assuming we don’t know exactly what kind of load

03:07 out our shooter is packing, then let’s instead  focus on the next majorly important factor:

03:12 the bullet itself. When a bullet is fired and  hits a human body, all that energy behind it

03:17 is transferred onto you, the unlucky target.  Wherever it strikes the body is where the energy

03:22 is transferred to, and that tapered end means  it’s all focused onto a small point. This is what

03:27 causes direct damage to the body, as that pointed  end has enough momentum behind it not just to

03:33 break the skin, but to penetrate tissue and bone. Now, all that energy, concentrated into pushing

03:39 the point of that bullet through your head. Let’s  say you were directly facing the shooter when they

03:43 fired. That means the bullet is now spinning  through the air with enough kinetic energy to

03:47 break through the skin of your forehead and into  the epicranial aponeurosis – the dense fibrous

03:53 tissue that covers the upper part of your skull. By now, you might be thinking what kind of damage

03:57 you’d receive from a gunshot to the head? Or  rather, you would be, if you hadn’t just been

04:01 shot. Well, bullets can damage flesh and organs in  a few different ways - the first of which coming

04:06 as a result of a direct hit. This causes a bullet  to leave a permanent cavity in whatever is in its

04:11 path, which in this case happens to be you and  the contents of your head: namely your brain. So,

04:16 you’d likely be on the receiving end of what's  known as a TBI, or a traumatic brain injury.

04:22 In most urban areas across the U.S., gunshot  wounds are a leading cause of TBI’s. Roughly

04:27 12% of all TBIs are linked to firearms - whether  from violent assaults or accidental discharges.

04:32 And gunshot wounds to the head account for  about 35% of all TBI-related deaths. But,

04:38 if you’re thinking that means you have a 65%  per cent chance of survival, think again.

04:43 Gunshot wounds to the head are fatal around 90%of  the time, with most victims dying on the scene,

04:49 if not instantly. Though some victims can  survive the initial trauma – including one

04:53 we’ll talk about shortly – around half of these  survivors will die in the emergency room. So,

04:58 safe to say, your odds of sustaining a traumatic  brain injury? Pretty high. Odds of you surviving

05:02 it? Not so much. But what exactly causes  someone to die from a gunshot wound?

05:07 A wound where a bullet enters the body – or in  your case, the cranium – but does not travel far

05:13 enough to exit is referred to as a ‘penetrating  wound’. If a bullet is able to travel fast and far

05:18 enough through to exit the body, this is called  a ‘perforating wound’ - also known as a ‘through

05:23 and through’. In either instance, you’ve still  got a high velocity metal projectile penetrating

05:28 and travelling through your brain tissue. But  what an impact like this also causes is a wave

05:33 of pressure to be transmitted through that brain  tissue. The resultant damage from this pressure

05:38 wave – as well as the bleeding – can cause the  brain to swell, leading to a TBI and death.

05:44 There’s another type of injury that can also  occur when being shot, and that’s caused by

05:48 the shock waves of the bullet’s impact. Any  tissue surrounding the bullet as it travels

05:52 on its path can become caught up in a temporary  vacuum, created by the high speed and velocity of

05:57 the projectile. This vacuum can be forty times  the size of the actual bullet itself, warping

06:03 and stretching any tissue caught in its path. As the bullet burrows deep - or passes clean

06:08 through - it rips apart tissue, bursts blood  vessels, and unleashes a surge of pressure

06:13 inside your skull. But there’s also shockwaves  that are coming off the bullet. They ripple

06:18 outward from the bullet’s path like waves across  a pond, distorting and stretching brain matter in

06:23 every direction. And if that wasn’t bad enough,  some bullets can fragment on impact. This causes

06:29 small, sharp pieces of metal to become lodged  throughout any tissue the bullet passes through.

06:33 The severity of an injury and the extent of the  damage left by a gunshot wound to the head can

06:39 vary depending on the location. If the bullet  passes through the tip of your right frontal

06:43 lobe - just behind the forehead - and avoids the  base of the skull, you might actually be “lucky.”

06:49 That’s because this area doesn’t house as many  vital brain functions or major blood vessels as

06:54 deeper regions. But that still doesn’t guarantee  you’d survive the injury inflicted though.

06:59 If a bullet enters through the tip of your  left frontal lobe and travels downward toward

07:03 the temporal lobe and brainstem - then that’s a  different story. It would be travelling through

07:08 some of the most vital tissue inside your  head. That’s more likely to be lights out,

07:12 permanently. The same goes for if a bullet’s  trajectory went through any of the key blood

07:16 vessels in your brain. This could result in  a blood clot, which would rapidly expand,

07:21 compressing the vital tissues of your brain. If  that happens, you’re either dead on the scene,

07:26 or battling against more of that rapidly  increasing pressure inside your skull.

07:30 Whichever way you slice it, it’s not looking good.  If the bullet doesn’t directly penetrate your

07:35 vital brain tissue shortly after impact, then any  one of the resultant injuries will likely finish

07:40 you off… unless you happen to be extremely lucky. Remember how we mentioned some gunshot victims

07:46 survive their initial wound? Well, one of those  was 14-year-old Ahad Israfil, who was shot in the

07:51 head as the result of a freak accident. In 1987  while at work, Ahad’s employer allegedly knocked

07:57 a firearm onto the floor, which caused the weapon  to discharge. The bullet struck Ahad in the head,

08:03 destroying much of his brain tissue - in  particular his right cerebral hemisphere,

08:07 along with the right half of his skull.  He was immediately rushed to hospital,

08:11 where intensive care surgeons tried to save  his life. To their amazement, after five hours,

08:16 Ahad regained consciousness and tried to speak. The skin covering Ahad’s scalp actually survived

08:22 the injury, and plastic surgeons were able to  use a silicon implant to fill the resultant

08:27 hole in his skull - where the right half  of his brain had been. The skin was then

08:31 stretched over this implant to give Ahad more  of a natural appearance - the repairs to his

08:35 scalp meant he could even regrow his hair. But  if you’re thinking that Ahad lived a difficult

08:40 life missing half of his brain, think again. When a bullet damages someone’s right hemisphere,

08:45 this can leave the victim with motor and sensory  impairments on the left side of their body,

08:49 and vice versa. Functions like thought,  memory, speech and vision are controlled

08:53 by both sides of the brain working in tandem.  So, damaging one hemisphere can mean that

08:58 someone is still able to perform some of these  functions, more often in a limited capacity.

09:03 Incredibly though, Ahad Israfil not only regained  most of his mental faculties and is able to speak,

09:09 he even successfully obtained an honours  degree from his local university. He lived

09:14 a long life afterwards, eventually passing  away in an Ohio nursing home back in 2019,

09:18 over 30 years after surviving his traumatic  brain injury. His is a pretty remarkable

09:23 story and a great example of the human brain’s  capacity to recover even from severe injuries.

09:29 But if we were in your shoes, we wouldn’t exactly  put all our chips on miraculously getting better

09:34 after being shot in the head. You need a lot  of things on the bingo card in order to survive

09:39 a wound like that, but hey, maybe you get lucky. So long as the bullet entry point and exit wounds

09:44 aren’t too severe, and the bullet misses the  critical areas of the brain. It also needs to be

09:49 a low-caliber round, fired from a lower-velocity  weapon and the shooter can’t be too close.

09:54 You’d need immediate, high-quality medical  treatment, be in good health - not too old,

09:59 no major medical conditions - and your blood  pressure should be stable. And you don’t end up

10:03 with one of the several possible resultant  internal injuries from the gunshot… then

10:08 maybe survival would be on the cards for you. Think you'd survive a shot to the head? What

10:11 surprised you the most? Drop your thoughts below. No go check out What Happens When You Die?

10:13 or click on this video instead.
