docs.text:
00:00 73 seconds after launch.

00:02 The Challenger space shuttle rises higher and  higher toward space. Its iconic white solid rocket

00:07 boosters roar as flames spew out the back of them.  The flight crew has continued to communicate with

00:12 launch control since lift-off. No one knows that  anything is wrong and that in the next second,

00:16 tragedy will strike. A fire rages along the  side of the right booster as fuel escapes

00:21 due to a compromised seal. In moments, the  supporting struts connecting the rockets to

00:26 the orange external fuel tank will experience a  catastrophic failure. The booster will slam into

00:31 the tank. The rocket fuel will ignite,  and there will be a massive explosion.

00:35 April 4, 1983: T minus 2 years and 9  months until the Challenger disaster.

00:41 “All systems go. Prepare for liftoff,” mission  control says over the intercom to the Challenger

00:46 flight crew. This will be the space shuttle's  maiden voyage. The boosters ignite, and the184

00:51 foot, 4.5-million-pound space shuttle thrusts  toward space. The first mission was a success,

00:57 and the Challenger space shuttle will end up  flying 6 more missions that year. The shuttle

01:01 is reliable, but every time it launches into  space and lands after re-entry, a toll is taken

01:06 on the spacecraft. Constant repairs need to be  made while old components are swapped out for

01:11 new ones. Engineers who work on the shuttle day  in and day out warn NASA that the stresses that

01:16 constant missions to space place on the space  shuttle may lead to tragedy in the future.

01:21 July 19, 1985 T minus 6 months  until the Challenger disaster.

01:26 “We are pleased to inform you that you have  been selected to become the first teacher

01:30 to go to space.” Christa McAuliffe can’t believe  the words she has just read. Several months ago,

01:36 she submitted her application to the  NASA Teacher in Space Project along with

01:41 11,000 other educators. Never in her wildest  dreams did she believe she would be chosen.

01:45 However, this letter confirms that she will, in  fact, be going to space and that she will be lucky

01:50 enough to share this incredible experience with  students across the country when she gets back.

01:55 McAuliffe teaches at Concord High  School in New Hampshire. When she

01:58 tells her colleagues the news, they  are elated. Her family, friends,

02:02 and students are all extremely happy for her.  As a part of the Teacher in Space Project,

02:06 she will conduct two lessons from orbit and embark  on a lecture series across the United States to

02:11 share her experience with students. This will  be done to highlight the importance of teachers

02:16 in the country and hopefully inspire students  to pursue careers in technology and science.

02:20 Over the next several months, McAuliffe  joins her fellow crewmates at Johnson

02:24 Space Center in Houston, Texas, where they  train and prepare for their coming mission.

02:28 Francis R. Scobee will be the commander  of the spacecraft. In April of 1984,

02:33 he piloted Challenger mission STS-41-C which  deployed a new satellite and repaired a damaged

02:39 satellite before returning to Earth. Since then,  he has been an instructor pilot for the Shuttle's

02:43 747 carrier aircraft. This will be his first  space command, and he couldn’t be more excited.

02:49 Piloting the mission will be Michael J. Smith.  He has flown 28 different types of civilian and

02:54 military aircraft and logged 4,867 hours  of flight time. Judith A. Resnik will be

03:00 one of the mission specialists on board.  Resnik had been part of Astronaut Group 8,

03:04 which was the first to include women on the  team. She has developed a variety of software

03:09 and procedures that are utilized throughout  NASA. She has been to space before aboard

03:13 the STS-41-D mission in August 1984. This was the  very first mission of the space shuttle Discovery.

03:19 Two other mission specialists are a  part of the Challenger crew as well.

03:22 Ronald E. McNair flew aboard Challenger in  February 1984 during mission STS-41-B. It

03:29 was on this mission that he became the second  African American man to fly in space. Ellison

03:33 S. Onizuka was the first Asian American  and the first person of Japanese origin

03:38 to reach space during his time aboard the  space shuttle Discovery during STS-51-C.

03:43 The final crew member aboard the upcoming  Challenger launch designated STS-51-L is

03:48 Gregory B. Jarvis. He’s the payload specialist.  This will be his first time in space, although

03:53 he had been slated to fly aboard a different  shuttle in April of 1985, but his spot was given

03:59 to U.S. senator Jake Garn instead. Then a similar  situation happened again in early January 1986

04:05 when U.S. representative Bill Nelson took his  place aboard another space shuttle. Now Jarvis

04:10 finally has the opportunity to reach space where  he can put his astronaut training to good use.

04:15 But like every other member of the crew, he will  never actually make it beyond Earth’s atmosphere.

04:20 January 22, 1986: T minus 6 days  until the Challenger disaster.

04:25 The Challenger crew eagerly awaits confirmation  of whether their mission is a go or not. A

04:30 high-ranking NASA officer enters the room with  a frown on his face. “Sorry about this crew,

04:35 but we’re going to have to delay your mission  until 61-C gets back. Their assignment ran into

04:39 delays, and their shuttle isn’t due to land  until tomorrow.” The Challenger crew looks

04:43 at one another in dismay. They are eager to  get going. Every mission to space is special,

04:48 and even for veteran astronauts,  it’s what they dream about doing

04:51 every night. It’s as if the stars are  beckoning them to reach for the unknown.

04:55 January 27, 1986: T minus 1 day  until the Challenger disaster.

05:01 Challenger mission STS-51-L is planned to have  an early morning lift-off the following day.

05:06 The astronauts toss and turn in their beds in  anticipation. A chill sweeps across Florida

05:11 as if foreshadowing the ominous events that  will happen in the coming hours. The launch

05:15 pad becomes covered in thick ice; the metals  that make up the space shuttle and boosters

05:20 contract slightly with the cold. As engineers  check the spacecraft over and over again to

05:24 make sure it’s in an acceptable condition for  launch, a disturbing realization surfaces.

05:29 “Sir, I want to reiterate that I am concerned  about the reliability of the seals in the

05:33 rockets,” an engineer explains to  his superior. For over two years,

05:37 the engineers and technicians that work  in the shuttle program have warned that

05:40 the space shuttles are being overused.  The crafts are sturdy and well made,

05:44 but every machine has its breaking point,  and it feels as if, after dozens of flights,

05:49 it’s only a matter of time before something  tragic happens. The NASA official acknowledges

05:53 the engineer's concern but does nothing  more. The launch will commence as scheduled,

05:58 regardless of the warnings voiced by the men  and women working directly with the spacecraft.

06:02 January 28, 1986: 9:00 a.m.: T minus 2 hours  and 38 minutes until the Challenger disaster.

06:09 The sun is rising higher and higher over the  Atlantic Ocean. A crowd gathers around Cape

06:14 Canaveral to watch the launch at Kennedy Space  Center scheduled for later that morning. There

06:18 are members of the press, local residents, and  people who have traveled from around the world

06:22 to watch the launch. Many are there to witness  the historic event of the first teacher to go

06:27 to space. Excitement and anticipation fill  the air. This will be the 25th space shuttle

06:32 launch and the 10th Challenger mission.  All other flights have been successful,

06:36 so there is no reason to suspect  today should be any different.

06:39 The astronauts don their suits and proceed  to their launch vehicle. They are greeted by

06:44 cheers as they step off their transport and  proceed towards the elevator that will carry

06:48 them to the cockpit of the Challenger.  Mission control in Houston prepares to

06:51 track and monitor the space shuttle's progress.  Telemetry coming in from hundreds of sensors is

06:56 recorded and double-checked to make sure that  Challenger is ready. The astronauts strap in,

07:01 and the shuttle door is sealed behind them.  The cockpit is quiet except for the sounds

07:05 of switches being engaged while Socbee and  Smith check the systems on board. There is

07:09 a sense of anxiousness, excitement, and pride  as the seven-person crew prepares for launch.

07:14 McAuliffe looks out the window directly  ahead of her at the blue sky. Just beyond

07:18 the atmosphere lies the edge of space. A bird  flies pasts; McAuliffe smiles. Soon she will

07:24 be doing something that only a handful  of people in all of history have done.

07:27 She checks her safety harness and leans  back in her seat, releasing a long sigh.

07:32 Besides the crew, the shuttle also  carries a Tracking and Data Relay

07:36 Satellite designated TDRS-B. Also in the  cargo bay is the Spartan Halley spacecraft,

07:41 which is designed to be released from Challenger  to study Halley’s Comet for two days while the

07:46 celestial object approaches the sun. The small  satellite will then be picked up by the Challenger

07:50 crew and brought back to Earth so scientists can  analyze the data it has collected. Tragically,

07:55 no one and nothing aboard Challenger will  survive to perform this series of tests.

07:59 January 28, 1986: 11:38: T  minus 10 seconds until launch.

08:06 Due to weather conditions, the launch  has been delayed yet again. However,

08:09 the atmosphere is beginning to  cooperate. The sky clears up,

08:12 and the wind clams. Commander Scobee and Pilot  Smith check their sensors and instruments one

08:17 last time as they prepare for the rockets to fire.  Mission control reaches the end of its countdown.

08:22 10. 9. 8. 7. 6. We have main engine  start. 4. 3. 2. 1 and liftoff.

08:32 Moments before the engines ignite and the space  shuttle rises, the solid rocket ignition command

08:38 is sent. The boosters roar to life. The space  shuttle and earth around the launchpad begin

08:42 to shake. The sound travels across the water and  reaches the bystanders watching the space shuttle

08:47 launch from miles away. Astronaut Judy Resnik is  heard over the intercom. “All right!” she yells.

08:52 Challenger Space Shuttle achieves liftoff.

08:55 After the rockets ignite eight 25-inch-long,  7-inch-wide exploding bolts fire. The Challenger

09:01 space shuttle is free to rise into the  sky. The deafening boom of the engines,

09:06 massive amounts of smoke, and intense heat roll  across the launch pad. A quarter of a second

09:11 after launch, sensors record the first vertical  motion of Challenger as it begins its ascent.

09:16 Unknown to anyone on board or at mission control,

09:18 an abnormal black smoke is seeping out of the  right solid rocket booster near the location of

09:24 one of the O-ring joints. This is the first sign  that something is about to go terribly wrong.

09:29 1 second after liftoff.

09:30 “Here we go!” Pilot Michael Smith  says over the intercom. As the space

09:35 shuttle proceeds toward the heavens, the  black smoke coming from the right rocket

09:38 seems to be slowing down.

3 seconds after liftoff.

09:41 Launch commentator Hugh Hariss has just finished  the countdown and pauses for a moment to watch.

09:46 He announces on NASA-SELECT television,  “Liftoff of the 25th space shuttle mission,

09:51 and it has cleared the tower." The  abnormal black smoke coming from

09:54 the bottom of the solid rocket booster  appears to have disappeared completely.

09:58 5 seconds after liftoff.

10:00 All systems go. There are no anomalies  detected by anyone at this point in the

10:04 launch. The three liquid-fueled main engines  on the back of the space shuttle are throttled

10:08 up from 90% to 104% thrust. Everything is  going according to plan. At mission control,

10:14 data processing systems engineer A.F. Algate  confirms liftoff. There is a cheer in the room

10:20 then everyone immediately goes back to monitoring  their stations. Suddenly, there is a data blackout

10:25 from the space shuttle. No one panics. This is to  be expected as the flames and structures around

10:30 the launch complex interfere with the radio  signals being sent to the antenna complex.

10:34 But there is one piece of data that is slightly  unnerving. “I’m reading the internal pressure

10:39 on the right-side booster to be 11.8 pounds  per square inch higher than normal,” one of

10:44 the technicians in mission control says. The  rocket is still within acceptable parameters,

10:48 but this initial data point will be used later on

10:51 to identify when the Challenger space  shuttle began to run into trouble.

10:54 8 seconds after liftoff.

10:56 Once Challenger is in the open air, Pilot  Smith begins a roll maneuver that puts the

11:01 crew in a heads down position so the top  of the space shuttle is pointing towards

11:04 the Earth and the bright orange external  fuel tank is towards the sky. "Houston,

11:08 Challenger. Roll program," Commander  Scobee says over the intercom.

11:12 "Roger roll, Challenger," Astronaut Dick  Covey says from mission control. "Good roll,

11:16 flight," Flight dynamics officer Brian  Perry confirms from the control room.

11:20 19 seconds after liftoff.

11:22 The Challenge space shuttle begins  to shake. There is a sudden violent

11:26 thrust to the side. The crew grits their  teeth as Michael Smith pulls on the flight

11:30 stick slightly. With the help of the NAV  system, the space shuttle realigns itself,

11:34 and Challenger is back on course. "Looks like  we've got a lot of wind here today,” says Smith

11:38 over the intercom. Commander Scobee confirms  the assessment. They begin throttling down the

11:42 three main engines of the space shuttle to 94%  thrust as planned at this point in the flight.

11:47 21 seconds after liftoff.

11:49 Challenger’s roll maneuver is completed,  and all systems confirm it is on the proper

11:54 trajectory to reach orbit. Commander  Scobee looks out the cockpit window,

11:57 hoping to get a glimpse of the land  below. "It's a little hard to see

12:00 out my window here,” he says. The  engines continue to throttle down.

12:04 28 seconds after liftoff.

12:06 "There's 10,000 feet, and Mach point  five,” Smith says over the intercom.

12:10 Challenger is now traveling at half the speed  of sound and is 10,000 feet above the surface

12:15 of the planet. It’s at this point that the  space shuttle begins reaching the region of

12:19 maximum aerodynamic pressure. Mission control  confirms that engines are throttling down to

12:24 94% and remind the flight crew that they will be  throttling down to 65% thrust in a few seconds.

12:29 35 seconds after liftoff.

12:31 Smith begins to throttle down the engines some  more. All data indicates that the shuttle’s

12:36 computer systems are making the proper adjustments  to deal with the wind shear. 5 seconds later,

12:40 Smith confirms that they have reached  Mach 1. Scobee adds that they are passing

12:45 19,000 feet in altitude.

45 seconds after liftoff.

12:48 There is a bright flash slightly behind the  space shuttle’s right wing. Moments later,

12:52 there is a second bright flash.

12:54 48 seconds after liftoff.

12:56 A third flash appears downstream  of Challenger's right wing.

12:59 The crew can’t see these ominous explosions,  but a 70-millimeter tracking camera captures

13:04 them as it zooms in on the shuttle for  a close-up view. Everyone who is viewing

13:08 the footage is baffled at what they are  witnessing. Suddenly an orange ball of

13:12 flames erupts from under the right wing. This  fireball is coming from the right booster.

13:16 The Challenger crew and mission control  have no idea that anything is wrong as

13:21 the space shuttle’s telemetry  all reads nominal. The fireball

13:24 from under the wing merges with the  flames of the solid rocket boosters.

13:27 58 seconds after liftoff.

13:29 Challenger accelerates past 1,539 miles per  hour or 2,477 kilometers per hour. It has an

13:37 altitude of 26,127 feet or 7,963.5 meters.  Scobee gives the command to throttle the

13:45 engines back as planned. Smith confirms the  command. Mission control confirms that the

13:50 three engines of the space shuttle  have throttled down to 65% thrust.

13:54 While this is happening, the tracking  camera on the ground observes the first

13:58 evidence that there is now something seriously  wrong with the right solid rocket booster. An

14:03 abnormal plume of smoke has begun pouring  out of the rocket. The Challenger crew has

14:07 no sensors in the cockpit that display the  performance of the solid rocket boosters and,

14:11 therefore, are unaware that  they are in serious danger.

14:14 A second later, Challenger passes through the  region of maximum aerodynamic pressure, which

14:19 pushes against the space shuttle and its boosters  with 720 pounds of pressure per square foot or

14:25 7,750 pounds per square meter. The plume of smoke  coming from the side of the booster intensifies.

14:31 Inside the booster itself, an O-ring has  disintegrated, the very same component

14:37 that engineers at NASA were warning would fail  if the space shuttle launches were not dialed

14:42 back. The O-ring on the booster was meant  to seal the joints between separate parts

14:45 of the rocket and prevent the leaking  of fluids and gasses from one chamber

14:49 to another. With the O-ring destroyed, fuel  is making its way through the booster and

14:54 igniting due to the intense heat of the flames.  A continuous inferno is expelled from the right

14:59 booster along the side furthest away from the  space shuttle. The windows in the cockpit give

15:03 Scobee and Smith limited visibility, and they  are not able to see the fire from the shuttle.

15:08 60 seconds after liftoff.

15:10 "Feel that mother go!" Smith says over the  intercom. Another member of the crew is heard

15:15 yelling with joy in the background. At that  moment, mission control receives data that

15:19 indicates the internal pressure in the right  side solid rocket booster has begun to drop.

15:24 It’s not known at the time, but this severe drop  in pressure is the result of the hole created by

15:28 the ignited fuel spewing out the side of  the rocket where the O-ring has failed.

15:33 The flames pouring out of the side of  the rocket begin to lick the fitting

15:36 attachments that couple the back end of the  booster to the external fuel tank on the

15:40 underside of the space shuttle. This starts  to degrade the integrity of the couplings.

15:44 62 seconds after liftoff.

15:46 Challenger shudders once again from high  wind speeds. The shuttle rolls slightly

15:51 to compensate as it passes 35,000 feet and  approaches Mach 1.5. The wind is worse than

15:57 predicted and stronger than any of the  previous 24 shuttle missions. However,

16:01 it’s still within acceptable limits, even if  it puts slightly more stress on the shuttle.

16:05 64 seconds after liftoff.

16:08 The flame in the right side booster changes shape  suddenly as the heat from the fire melts through

16:13 metal plating, and liquid hydrogen begins  to fuel the fire. The glow on the outside of

16:18 the booster intensifies. As the force of the  raging fire builds up, it begins to move the

16:22 engine nozzle in large arcs. This momentum  begins to shift the space shuttles course,

16:27 which the computer then adjusts for. The  right booster’s thrust levels are thrown

16:31 off due to the leaking fuel and fire burning  on the side. However, the NAV system manages

16:36 to compensate. Tremors vibrate through the  cockpit as the hydrogen fuel is ignited but

16:41 gets lost in the turbulence experienced due  to the massive acceleration and wind sheers.

16:46 66 seconds after liftoff.

16:48 "Throttle up, three at 104,” mission control says  over the com. Houston and the Challenger flight

16:53 crew are still unaware of the fire coming  out of the middle of the right booster,

16:57 and other than a drop in pressure, there is no  indication that there is a serious problem. The

17:01 fire outside of the shuttle spread further. The  flames creep toward the belly of the shuttle,

17:05 where the external liquid hydrogen tank  is located. The pressure inside the fuel

17:09 tank suddenly begins to drop, indicating that an  alarming amount of liquid hydrogen is leaking out.

17:15 The fuel tank gauge plummets inside the cockpit,

17:18 but Smith and Scobee don’t notice it as they  are focused on throttling up the engines and

17:22 preparing to disengage the boosters. Even if  either crewmember was looking at the fuel gauge,

17:27 the rapid dropping of pressure happened so  quickly that there was nothing they could have

17:31 done. The fuel tank can only be disengaged  when all other engines are turned off,

17:35 and the shuttle is in a benign aerodynamic  environment higher up in the atmosphere. If

17:40 they had disengaged the fuel tank to get away  from the leak at this stage, the Challenger

17:44 would have been forced into the fuel tank and  the still-burning solid rocket booster exhaust.

17:49 68 seconds after liftoff.

17:51 The fire spewing from the side of the  rocket connects to the exhaust plume.

17:55 The liquid oxygen propellant being fed into  the main engines of the space shuttle falls

17:59 drastically. Smith continues to throttle  up the engines to reach 104% thrust.

18:04 72 seconds after liftoff.

18:06 The back end of the right booster is ripped  away from the external fuel tank. The strut

18:11 that had been securing it has been compromised  and failed. The back end of the right booster is

18:16 now moving up and down relative to the space  shuttle and fuel tank. Another explosion,

18:20 likely from the stress and leaking  fuel, occurs higher up on the booster

18:24 near Challenger’s cabin. The flame near  the top of the booster grows rapidly,

18:28 creating an enormous fireball. The nozzles of  the engines on the back of the space shuttle

18:32 begin moving at a rate of 5 feet per second in  order to compensate for the unhinged booster.

18:37 The top of the right booster is  still connected to the fuel tank,

18:40 but the loose back end causes a burst  of lateral acceleration that jerks

18:44 the shuttle. The main engine pressure  decreases. Engine nozzle motion rates

18:48 are off the chart. Things are very, very bad.  Challenger sends its final navigation update.

18:54 73 seconds after liftoff.

18:56 “Uh oh…” Smith says. These will be the last words  uttered over the comms by any of the Challenger

19:02 crew. It’s not clear what Smith is referring  to, but it’s likely that several sensors begin

19:06 showing clear signs that something is wrong. The  fuel tank and loose booster begin breaking apart.

19:11 The shuttle jerks the opposite way it had moments  before. The right booster is now producing 100,000

19:17 pounds of thrust less than the left booster.  The unbalanced acceleration begins forcing

19:22 the right booster up into the liquid  oxygen section of the external fuel tank.

19:26 Liquid hydrogen and oxygen begin leaking out of  the external tank. A cloud of fuel accumulates

19:31 outside. The right-side booster pushes  further into the fuel tank and increases

19:36 the amount of liquid oxygen being expelled.  Milliseconds later, the inevitable happens.

19:40 There is a bright flash of light located between  the Challenger shuttle and the external fuel tank.

19:46 The leaking fuel has been ignited. The fireball  engulfs the space shuttle. There is a crackling

19:51 sound over the intercom as ground transmitters  search for a signal that is no longer there.

19:55 Another explosion occurs near the front of the  external fuel tank. This ignites the remainder of

20:00 the fuel inside the front section of the tank,  causing it to detonate. Challenger’s engines

20:05 redline and the computer initiates an emergency  shutdown. Main engine 3 goes first, followed by

20:11 number 1. The last telemetry signal from the space  shuttle is sent while it is being torn apart.

20:16 74 seconds after liftoff.

20:18 The radio signal from Challenger goes silent.

20:21 Another explosion occurs near the space shuttle's  nose. The cockpit with all seven members of the

20:26 crew is engulfed in flames as the rocket fuel  in the forward reaction control system ignites.

20:31 The debris of the destroyed shuttle continues  traveling upward at Mach 1.92, or approximately

20:36 twice the speed of sound. It reaches an altitude  of 46,000 feet or 14,021 meters. Challenger’s tail

20:43 emerges from the fireball around the same moment  that a wing can be seen. The fuselage and payload

20:48 bay are torn apart by the rush of air forced in  from the tail being ripped off, overpressurizing

20:53 the payload bay and breaking it apart from the  inside out. Wires and electrical cables flail

20:58 behind the fuselage like tentacles. The satellites  in the cargo bay are ejected into the air.

21:03 The crew cabin arcs out of the flames  and smoke. It seems to be intact,

21:07 although there is a gaping hole where it  used to be connected to the rest of the

21:11 shuttle. Some of the crew may still be alive and  awake, but when the Challenger is ripped apart,

21:15 all of the air is sucked out of the cockpit,  and a dramatic pressure drops results in

21:19 everyone passing out. For this mission, the  astronauts did not wear pressurized suits

21:24 during liftoff. As they slump in their seats  unconscious, oxygen deprivation settles in.

21:29 Any crewmember who is still alive will  suffocate within the next few minutes.

21:33 The two solid rocket boosters continue  to fly upwards at different angles,

21:37 now free from the struts that connected  them to the external fuel tank.

21:40 1 second after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

21:43 Mission control does not yet know that the  Challenger space shuttle has exploded. "One

21:48 minute 15 seconds. Velocity 2,900 feet per second.  Altitude nine nautical miles. Downrange distance

21:54 seven nautical miles," says Stephen Nesbitt,  the public affairs officer at mission control.

21:59 2 seconds after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

22:02 A parachute emerges from the carnage, giving  people hope. But as the tracking camera focuses,

22:07 it turns out to be the nose cap of the  right solid rocket booster. Smoke and

22:11 flaming debris arc outward from the blast.  The rocket boosters continue to fly upward,

22:15 leaving a corkscrew trail of smoke behind them.

22:18 15 seconds after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

22:21 "Flight, GC, we've had negative contact,  loss of downlink," says ground control

22:26 engineer N.R. Talbott. It’s at this  point that mission control is aware

22:29 something tragic has happened and  is trying to figure out exactly

22:32 what happened. They are informed that the  Challenger space shuttle has been lost.

22:36 36 seconds after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

22:39 A self-destruct signal is sent to the  rogue solid rocket boosters triggering

22:43 an emergency detonation. Both rockets explode  in a plume of black smoke. Debris falls back

22:48 towards the Earth. Without the weight  of the space shuttle and fuel tank,

22:51 there was no telling how far the rockets  would have gone before burning the last

22:55 of their fuel. They needed to be detonated  to eliminate the risk of them crashing back

22:59 to Earth in a populated area rather than in  the desolate waters of the Atlantic Ocean.

23:04 1 minute and 31 seconds after the  Challenger space shuttle explodes.

23:07 Multiple sources have now confirmed

23:10 that Challenger STS-51-L has been  lost. Rescue efforts are launched.

23:14 2 minutes and 11 seconds after the  Challenger space shuttle explodes.

23:18 The TV tracking camera spots the first pieces  of the space shuttle crashing into the ocean.

23:22 33 seconds later, the crew cabin slams into  the waves of the Atlantic at approximately 200

23:28 miles per hour or 322 kilometers per hour. At a  breaking force 200 times that of normal gravity,

23:34 the crew cabin disintegrates on impact and  sinks 100 feet to the bottom of the ocean.

23:39 For the next few minutes, debris continues to  splash down into the ocean east of Patrick Air

23:44 Force Base. A cloud of brown smoke lingers  over the surface of the water as a result

23:48 of the hydrazine rocket fuel that covered the  wreckage as it entered the ocean. Mission control

23:53 pinpoints the crash site as being approximately  28.64 degrees North and 80.28 degrees West.

23:59 5 minutes after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

24:02 The broadcast on NASA television has been  eerily quiet as everyone tries to take in

24:07 what just happened. The camera view switches  from the ocean back to the grandstand at

24:11 the press site. Observers stand with their  backs to the camera, looking up at the sky,

24:14 where a white cloud of smoke still lingers.  White wisps of haze extend from the explosion

24:19 site like weeping willow vines indicating  where burning debris fell from the sky.

24:23 8 minutes and 5 seconds after the  Challenger space shuttle explodes.

24:27 "This is mission control, Houston. We are  coordinating with recovery forces in the field.

24:31 Range safety equipment, recovery vehicles intended  for the recovery of the SRBs in the general area,"

24:36 says Stephen Nesbitt in a somber voice. The  only thing left to do is go through the data,

24:41 recover as much of the space shuttle as  possible, and determine what caused the

24:45 horrific accident that led to the loss of 7  people aboard the Challenger space shuttle.

24:49 March 7, 1986, 1 month and 10 days after  the Challenger space shuttle disaster.

24:54 The USS Preserver bobs up and down in  the dark waters of the Atlantic Ocean.

24:59 A dive team has just been deployed to  scout the hypothesized location of the

25:03 Challenger cabin. The divers locate  the wreckage that was the front of

25:06 the space shuttle and confirm that the  bodies of the crew are still inside.

25:09 The aftermath of the Challenger  space shuttle disaster.

25:12 All space shuttles are immediately grounded, and  any upcoming launches are canceled pending a full

25:18 investigation of what happened to the Challenger.  NASA and a group of men appointed by President

25:22 Ronald Regan, known as the Rogers Commission,  begin looking into the chain of events that led to

25:27 the loss of the space shuttle and its crew. It’s  concluded that the space shuttles are being pushed

25:31 too hard, and the concerns of engineers working on  the crafts are being ignored or overlooked. What

25:37 it came down to was that NASA has been trying  to accomplish too much with too little funding.

25:42 The investigation also determines that  the two rubber O-rings, which led to

25:46 the fuel leak in the right booster and eventual  catastrophic explosion of the external fuel tank,

25:50 were compromised by the severe cold from  the night before the launch. Unfortunately,

25:55 even if the crew had been aware of a problem  at liftoff, there would have been no way for

25:59 them to avoid the disastrous consequences.  The space shuttle wouldn’t have been able

26:03 to survive a high-speed separation even if it was  attempted before the external fuel tank exploded.

26:08 On June 6, the report is given to the President,  who determines Marshall Space Flight Center in

26:13 Huntsville, Alabama, Morton Thiokol Inc.,  and NASA as a whole are responsible for the

26:18 Challenger disaster. Marshall Space Flight  Center constructed the shuttle boosters,

26:22 engines, and tank, while Morton Thiokol  manufactured and built the booster motors.

26:27 It’s also uncovered during the investigation from  several engineers who testify that they expressed

26:32 concerns specifically about the O-rings and their  seals to their supervisors for at least two years

26:37 prior to the loss of the Challenger. The Rogers  Commission recommends that communication between

26:42 engineers and NASA management be tightened,  quality control procedures be improved,

26:46 and several more checkpoints be added  to the shuttle safety advisory panel.

26:50 On September 29, 1988, the space shuttle Discovery  launches with five veteran astronauts on board.

26:56 This is the first mission since the Challenger  disaster. The space shuttle program lasts for

27:01 23 more years. On July 8, 2011, Atlantis launches  from Cape Canaveral. It will be the 135th space

27:08 shuttle mission. Atlantis lands on Jul 21, 2011,  marking the official end of the space shuttle era.

27:14 Two space shuttles were lost during the 30  years that they were in use. On February 1,

27:19 2003, Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated as  it reentered the atmosphere, and on January 28,

27:25 1986, Challenger exploded due to a faulty  O-ring. Both crafts held a crew of 7, all of

27:30 which were lost and all of which were heroes. Now watch “Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima and

27:35 Nagasaki (Minute by Minute)” Or check out “What  If USA Launched a Nuclear Bomb (Minute by Minute)”

01:00 this is work that I do like literally in

01:03 my day job, right? As a psychiatrist, my

01:05 job is to take people who are moderately

01:07 successful and help them become

01:09 incredibly successful. In my day job as

01:11 a psychiatrist, my goal is to help

01:14 people shape their thinking in the

01:16 correct way. And the blunt unfortunate

01:18 truth is that I've learned you can't

01:20 control your thinking. And I'll give you

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 In October of 1347, 12 ships dropped anchor at a Sicilian port.

00:05 Those who eagerly approached were met with a grisly sight.

00:08 Almost all aboard were either dead or barely alive, their skin erupting with blackened

00:14 boils that dripped blood and pus.

00:16 In horror, the Sicilian authorities demanded the ships set sail, but though they left,

00:22 the damage had already been done.

00:23 The Black Death was now in Europe and millions would die in what is considered one of the

00:28 greatest disasters in history.

00:30 Let’s explore how the bubonic plague wiped out at least a third of Europe’s population,

00:35 if not more, in this episode of the Infographics Show, What Made the Black Death so Deadly?

00:41 Europe was hit hard by the plague, but it was not hit first.

00:44 It was also not unaware of a disease that was already bringing widespread death and

00:48 destruction elsewhere.

00:50 Before the infested ships arrived in Sicily rumors of a frightful sickness devastating

00:55 the populations of first China and then India, Egypt, Persia, and Syria had spread near and

01:00 far.

01:01 While no one knew what caused it or why, it seemed to follow trade routes spanning the

01:06 Near and Far East.

01:08 Further, when it appeared, it was by all accounts unstoppable.

01:12 Those struck by the Black Death would begin to swell at the lymph nodes located in their

01:16 groin area or under arm regions.

01:18 The growths would soon develop into large blackish blue egg-sized lumps, or for the

01:23 even less fortunate, expand to the size of apples.

01:26 These would then fester and ooze various bodily fluids.

01:29 Beyond this, those with the disease could develop any combination of a series of additional

01:34 symptoms.

01:35 These included fever, pain, chills, sweating, upset stomach, and diarrhea.

01:40 Almost always, this was followed by death.

01:43 According to those who observed its effects first-hand, all it appeared to take was brief

01:47 physical contact with the clothing of someone who was sick to pass the disease on to another.

01:52 Though, some doctors claimed that it was the spirit leaving the body of the deceased that

01:56 infected others as it passed by.

01:59 Obviously, at this point in history the real methods of disease transmission were not yet

02:03 well understood.

02:04 Without understanding it, most were helpless to defend against it.

02:07 Few areas other than some islands cut off from the rest of Europe by the sea made it

02:12 through the pandemic plague-free.

02:14 The rest of the population was not so lucky.

02:16 The bacterium infiltrated virtually every European city’s defenses and many who appeared

02:21 perfectly healthy one day could be dead a few days later.

02:25 It was uncommon though possible for someone to survive a week or two before he or she

02:30 died.

02:31 Compounding problems further, those with the disease would typically be asymptomatic for

02:35 the first few days and so no one would be aware that they had caught it.

02:38 This meant that successfully isolating them from the rest of society at this point was

02:42 all but impossible.

02:44 Those who tried the next best thing to protect themselves by fleeing for the country were

02:48 not safe there either.

02:49 The plague decimated livestock as well and countless pigs, cows, chickens, goats, and

02:54 sheep who also died a brutal death.

02:57 This was such a problem that it led to a shortage of wool throughout the continent.

03:01 While many European areas had a death figure of around 30%, 90% of the Italian city of

03:07 Florence perished.

03:08 Sometimes, bodies of the deceased remained where they had died as there were not enough

03:12 people still living to bury them.

03:14 Thousands of French villages in addition to areas in other locations were left without

03:18 a single remaining soul.

03:20 The Black Death had mercilessly transformed them into ghost towns.

03:24 In some instances, nature eventually took over, and areas that people once called home

03:29 were re-claimed by surrounding forest.

03:31 It took aerial photography following the end of World War I to rediscover these locations

03:36 as places where men, women, and children once lived.

03:39 Most estimates place Europe’s death total between 50 and 70 million, or around thirty-some

03:44 percent, though the CDC claims it killed as much as 60% of the population, which is considerably

03:50 more.

03:51 World-wide estimates typically range from 155 to 200 million.

03:55 The world at the time was a mere 500 million people, so nearly half of all of its’ inhabitants,

04:01 or again according to some sources even more, were killed.

04:04 So how was it that the Black Death was able to spread so quickly and wipe out so many,

04:09 people and animals alike?

04:11 Well for one, as previously mentioned, there was little in the way of scientific knowledge

04:15 in the 1300s.

04:16 Not only did people not understand the plague’s causes or modes of transmission, but there

04:21 were also countless failures in how those in the medical field attempted to treat it.

04:26 It is true that Yersina pestis, the bacterium behind the Black Death, or bubonic plague,

04:30 is highly contagious.

04:32 It can also be spread in many ways, though obviously contaminated spirits aren’t one

04:37 of them.

04:38 Many believe that in its later stages it had the ability to morph into an airborne strain

04:42 that could be passed on to a new host via a simple sneeze or cough.

04:45 However, all strains, airborne or those in the more initial stages that are not, are

04:50 believed to have been transferred through flea or lice bites.

04:53 And many animals in addition to countryside livestock serve as hosts for the bacterium

04:58 and blood sucking pests.

04:59 Examples are things like squirrels, rabbits, chipmunks, and mice.

05:03 However, many in the scientific field have argued that by far the worst contributor to

05:07 the spread of the Black Death was the urban rat and its flea.

05:11 Part of the reason for this belief is that rats have been observed to develop symptoms

05:15 quite similar to those in people, and in cases of the modern-day plague many people with

05:19 the sickness had accompanying bites from fleas.

05:22 Recent outbreaks often follow what’s known as ‘rat falls’ as well, or when the rodents

05:27 die off in record amounts for whatever reason.

05:29 Thus, the most prevalent theory is that the Black Death all began when rats with the plague

05:34 died and their fleas then looked for more blood in another readily available source,

05:38 which would at times be human.

05:41 Upon being bitten by the contaminated flea this person would then be exposed to the deadly

05:45 bacteria.

05:46 Seemingly in support of this theory, ships during the mid-1300s were commonly infested

05:50 with the furry rodents who thrived in their dark.

05:53 moist environment.

05:54 And following the death ships’ arrival in Sicily the plague continued to spread further

05:58 following a trade route pattern, as it had previously in Asia, to other port locations

06:03 throughout Europe and as far down as North Africa.

06:06 However, more recently there have been some proposed tweaks to this rat-based theory.

06:11 As we just mentioned, the Black Death, after all, is not the only outbreak of the plague

06:15 in the world’s history.

06:16 There have been outbreaks before as well as after, and those that took place more recently

06:21 followed a different pattern entirely.

06:23 Europe’s black death spread much faster, and as far as historical records are concerned

06:27 there was no mention of a mass rat die-off in the days or months preceding it.

06:32 Now, some scientists suggest that it was human fleas and lice that were the true culprits

06:37 behind Europe’s version of the disease.

06:39 In this case fleas would bite infected people and then move on to others, one by one, who

06:43 happened to be in the nearby vicinity.

06:45 They describe the underlying mathematical model that a rat-flea spread follows is quite

06:49 different from a human-flea or lice one.

06:52 And, when information was plugged into simulations the human-flea model more closely matched

06:56 data from seven of nine plague-hit European cities.

07:00 Those with this newest evidence admit that the causes of the plague are surrounded by

07:04 ongoing controversy.

07:05 However, whether the fleas were of the human or rat variety, it is blood sucking pests

07:10 of one kind or another that likely passed it on successfully and so very quickly.

07:15 It also turns out that the Black Death may not have been causing mass devastation all

07:20 by itself.

07:21 When victims bodies were exhumed from mass graves in England anthrax spores were also

07:25 discovered along with them.

07:26 If anthrax was occurring at the same time as the plague this would definitely have made

07:31 things much worse.

07:33 Anthrax cannot only be passed by coming into contact with sweat, saliva, or tears but also

07:38 by mere skin contact.

07:40 In other words, at the time of the Black Death pandemic, people could have come down with

07:44 a life-threatening disease of one kind or another in pretty much every conceivable way.

07:49 It is possible anthrax and other diseases made people extra susceptible to the plague

07:53 due to already compromised immunity.

07:55 Also, it is possible that the body count of those claimed by the Black Death included

08:00 victims that actually died from anthrax or other diseases.

08:03 Beyond its quick transfer from host to host and the contributions of additional disease,

08:09 the way the Black Death was treated failed to help and may have actually helped kill

08:13 victims or spread it further unintentionally.

08:16 For example, at least initially, medical practitioners would do such things as perform bloodletting

08:20 on patients with the plague.

08:22 This is where they cut into veins or arteries in the necks or arms of those who were sick,

08:27 so that their blood flowed freely.

08:29 This procedure was nothing new and, in fact, dated back as far as to the times of ancient

08:34 Egypt and Greece.

08:35 Historical figures believed that to be healthy the body needed the right balance of blood,

08:39 phlegm, and bile.

08:41 Bloodletting was believed to correct a possible imbalance of too much blood which is what

08:45 caused the person to get sick.

08:48 Unfortunately, the procedure appeared to be as ineffective for the victims of the plague

08:51 as it was for Charles II or George Washington centuries later.

08:55 While Washington awoke with a sore throat and King Charles suffered a seizure, following

09:00 bloodletting treatment both died shortly thereafter.

09:03 Boil-lancing was another technique used as a form of treatment which was just how it

09:08 sounds.

09:09 Someone would essentially lance, or stick a pointy object, into the boils to drain them

09:13 of their gooey contents.

09:14 If this wasn’t done, they would only continue to grow larger and, in time.

09:18 poison their host due to the mass build-up of dead blood and pus.

09:22 Then again, popping them could also cause death due to toxic shock.

09:26 Beyond the patient likely dying, the boils contained highly contagious matter and possibly

09:30 spread the disease yet further.

09:32 Other methods such as the burning of various herbs or immersing the sick in vinegar or

09:36 rosewater were also, unsurprisingly, ineffective.

09:39 In time, after failure upon failure and in an attempt at self-preservation, many doctors

09:45 simply stopped accepting patients.

09:47 Even priests began refusing to perform last rites out of danger for their own safety.

09:52 Where man failed nature did little to help either.

09:55 Not only did people have little idea of how to handle the plague, but they were genetically

09:59 prone to succumbing to it.

10:01 Studies of the remains of the European population at the time determined that only 0.2% had

10:07 a gene that offered them any form of immunity.

10:10 The other 99.8% had none.

10:12 Since so many of those who were susceptible to the plague died from it, they did not pass

10:16 their genes on further to the following generations.

10:19 Many of those who did have the gene lived on to procreate.

10:22 This is why Caucasian Americans now have a 15% chance of having some resistance to the

10:27 disease.

10:28 This is pretty good news considering the modern form of the plague is still around today.

10:33 One encounter via the 12 so-called death ships would go on to wipe out men, women, and children

10:39 to such an extent that it would change the tide of history.

10:42 What do you think, was it passed on by human or rat fleas?

10:46 Let us know in the comments!

10:47 Also, be sure to check out our other video called Could the Black Death (The Plague)

10:51 Happen Again?!

10:52 Thanks for watching, and, as always, don’t forget to like, share, and

10:56 subscribe.

10:57 See you next time!

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: Why You Wouldn't Survive 1 Day in CECOT... World's Largest Mega Prison in El Salvador
Video Information

  • Video ID: mNlKWWgmpus

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 It’s 2023, you’re a hardened member of Mara  Salvatrucha - better known as the infamous

00:06 MS-13 - and the government of El Salvador has  just sentenced you to a fate worse than death.

00:12 You’re forced like cattle into the back  of a heavily armored vehicle; tight-packed

00:16 flesh covered in gang tattoos holds you in place.  There’s barely space in this scorching vehicle for

00:21 you and the others to breathe. The guards stripped  you and gave you an uncomfortable cavity search,

00:27 leaving you violated and humiliated in  nothing but a pair of white shorts. An

00:31 unsympathetic police barber shaved you bald,  row by row of hair, just like all the others.

00:37 If you raise your head in transit,

00:39 a guard barks at you in Spanish to  get your head down, you worthless dog!

00:43 He wields his nightstick. You get the  impression that there’s nothing he’d

00:46 like more than cracking open the back of your  skull, flecking the naked skin of your fellow

00:51 prisoners with your blood. Just to send a  single message: Where you’re going, you’re

00:56 not considered human anymore. You’re an animal,  and when animals misbehave, they get put down.

01:01 You bow your head again. A wise choice - There’ll  be plenty of beatings later, so why start early?

01:07 But before you disappear back into the  sea of anonymous prisoners, you see it:

01:11 A glowing fortress, wreathed in barbed wire  and illuminated by piercing floodlights. It

01:16 makes Alcatraz look like Disneyland. It makes  Rikers look like a resort in Cancun. Hell,

01:21 after a few years here, Guantanamo  Bay would look like a health retreat.

01:25 This is the Centro de Confinamiento del  Terrorismo, or the Terrorism Confinement

01:30 Center. We’ll call it CECOT. You won’t find  another prison like this anywhere in the world.

01:35 But you’re not being sent here alone. There  are trails of buses in front of and behind you,

01:41 like some almost endless centipede of human  misery. You’re just one tiny percentage

01:45 point in a statistic - A tidal wave of 2000  prisoners, all being transferred at once,

01:51 as part of El Salvador’s sweeping efforts to  bring the country’s gang activity to its knees.

01:56 At its worst in 2011, El Salvador was  considered the murder capital of the

02:00 world. Peaking at 71 murders per hundred thousand.  In 2015, that number had risen to over 100 deaths

02:06 per hundred thousand. One day even saw 62  people murdered in 24 hours. Gang violence

02:12 had completely overtaken the Central American  country. Year after year, brutal gang warfare

02:17 saw the army roaming the streets just to keep  the country from falling into total collapse.

02:22 The government needed to take drastic measures.

02:24 You’re about to enter one  of those drastic measures.

02:27 Opened in 2022, very few people have  had the chance to see inside CECOT,

02:31 aside from the flood of prisoners being sent  there - including you. The media are not

02:35 allowed in. Lawyers are not allowed in. Human  rights groups are not allowed in. It’s closed

02:41 down almost entirely to the outside world. All  that civilians know about the facility has been

02:46 gleaned from satellite imagery, footage that the  El Salvador government has filmed and released.

02:51 The buses grind to a halt in a large grid outside  the prison. Some deep animal part of you feels

02:57 like you’re outside a slaughterhouse, and your  skin begins prickling with panic. You were a

03:02 bad dude on the outside - a robber, a killer, an  unquestioning enforcer of one of El Salvador’s

03:08 most feared gangs. Here, you’re a frightened  little child again, wishing for your mommy.

03:14 But you don’t get your mommy. You get manhandled  out of the bus by a huge man in riot gear,

03:19 clapping you in long cuffs that bind your  hands behind your back and connect to your

03:23 legs. The same thing is happening to hundreds,  then thousands, of other men around you. You

03:28 feel a nightstick press against the back of  your neck and instinctively bend over before

03:33 they can even start applying pressure.  Good boy. That’ll serve you well here.

03:37 The guards bark orders and corral you inside  like sheep. Of course, you obey. You and all

03:42 the others are practically naked, and even if  you managed to overpower one of the riot squad

03:47 guards specifically trained to beat you into  a fine puree, an expert sniper in one of the

03:52 nearby guard towers would put a round through  your head before you even had time to fart.

03:57 Right now, there are estimated to be  around 16,000 men in CECOT. That would

04:01 max out most prisons around the world.  The second largest prison in the world,

04:05 Silivri Penitentiaries Campus in  Turkey, manages to host a population

04:09 of around 22,000 inmates. CECOT is built  to double that, with a capacity of 40,000.

04:16 Even getting to the prison is a challenge.  President Nayib Bukele wanted to build it

04:20 far away from civilization. There are  no towns or cities nearby. No public

04:25 buildings or schools. The prison itself has  its own water supply and electric generators,

04:30 meaning it has even less need to connect  with anyone or anything external. That’s

04:35 why you spent so many hours roasting with your  fellow convicts in the back of that prison bus.

04:40 As you’re dragged into the main hall and  forced to boy down in lines for inspection,

04:45 you find yourself wondering how  one prison complex could hold so

04:48 many people. And the answer to that  is simple: It’s unimaginably huge.

04:54 There are eight prison blocks covering around 57  acres total but the plot of land for the prison

04:59 is an enormous 410 acres total. There are 19  guard towers perched high above the complex,

05:05 surveying everything. There are four layers  of walls surrounding the prison blocks,

05:10 each one is nearly ten feet tall and two feet  thick, with coils of barbed wire draped over

05:15 the top. And of course, you can’t forget  about the 15,000-volt electric fence too.

05:21 Surveillance cameras are in operation  24/7 and cover practically every square

05:25 inch of the facility. Nothing happens  off-camera. Should a riot break out,

05:29 they have a fully stocked armory with racks  and racks of firearms as well as heavy riot

05:34 gear for their guards. Even the US army  would have a hard time storming CECOT.

05:39 And you’re just a common thug  for hire. You’ve got no hope,

05:42 buddy. So, what have you got to  look forward to now you’re here?

05:45 When you first arrive, prisoner or not, you’re  subject to an intense screening process. Even

05:50 if you’re not an inmate, the guards at  CECOT have large X-ray machines that scan

05:54 you from head to toe to look for contraband.  You’ll also be asked to disclose any tattoos,

05:59 and if you don’t, they have the right to strip  you to check for themselves. The gangs in El

06:03 Salvador have a culture of tattooing their  members to cement their allegiance for life.

06:07 If you’ve got gang ties, you’re not getting  in unless it’s in handcuffs and white shorts.

06:12 Once you’ve been scanned,  searched again, beaten down,

06:15 and noted in the prison inventory, it’s time  for your first night at CECOT to begin. Part

06:19 of you just feels relieved that you’ll  finally be able to sleep after what’s

06:23 felt like the longest day of your life - But  we’ve got some bad news for you there, too.

06:27 The guards organize you into groups by cell  block and chase you, your hands on your head,

06:32 your back bowed over. If you lag behind,  you might take a nightstick to the spine

06:36 or the ankle, or feel the electric  burn of a stun gun on your bare skin.

06:41 They run you like the bulls of Pamplona  until you reach your cell, at which point,

06:45 a swift kick to the ass sends you tumbling in,  the reinforced metal door slamming behind you

06:50 once all of the others assigned to  this cell have been trapped there,

06:53 too. This is when you start to notice a number  of horrifying things about your new home.

06:59 For starters, the lights are always on. They  don’t switch them off at night, they don’t even

07:03 dim them, they are on 24/7 at full blast. Bright  harsh artificial light floods every communal cell.

07:10 There are 80 beds to a cell. We say beds, they  have no mattresses or bedding on them. Instead,

07:15 they’re harsh bunk bed frames, stacked four  high, with nothing to lie on but flat metal.

07:21 In the corners of the cells, right by the bars,  are two toilets. Next to them are two wash basins,

07:26 but the flow of water in these  is controlled by a guard outside

07:29 the cell. So that’s 80 prisoners in a cell  sharing just two toilets. Except it isn’t.

07:35 It seems that El Salvador is actually  cramming more than 80 in each cell.

07:39 We hope you don’t mind having plenty of roommates.

07:41 When a BBC reporter asked the director of the  prison exactly what the capacity of CECOT was,

07:46 the man smiled and said “Where you  can fit 10 people, you can fit 20.”

07:50 Can you imagine a worse night’s  sleep? Being in a brightly lit cell,

07:54 with over 100 other people, all the most  hardened gangsters in Central America,

07:59 lying on a metal sheet, with two shared toilets  stinking out the cell. Human rights groups have

08:05 estimated that prisoners in CECOT have just  0.6 square meters of personal space each.

08:11 That number falls far below the 4 square  meters mandated in the European Union.

08:16 There are solitary confinement cells too,  and to many, they might be preferable,

08:21 but they’ve got their trade-offs  too. Instead of a metal bed frame,

08:24 you have a slab of concrete to lie on. You get  one toilet. One wash basin. And while the communal

08:29 cells are always bathed in artificial light, you  have the opposite problem. No light at all, either

08:35 artificial or natural, meaning you just have to  sit in darkness all day stewing in your thoughts.

08:41 And at CECOT, one thing is for sure:  You’re not having pleasant thoughts.

08:45 Before we tell you about the horrors that  await you when you wake up in the morning,

08:49 we’ve got an important question to  answer: Why does El Salvador need

08:53 such a massive prison? Who are the men  arriving here and when will they leave?

08:58 We mentioned earlier a particular day in  El Salvador when 62 people were killed.

09:03 This was the 26th of March 2022. It was the  bloodiest day in the country’s history and

09:08 the final straw for the Salvadoran people.  President Bukele announced a radical new

09:12 approach to combating gang warfare.  Have been nominated largely for his

09:16 tough stance on gangs back in 2019, it was time  for him to put his money where his mouth was.

09:22 His plan was a sweeping raft of changes  that removed almost all of the barriers

09:26 preventing the police from arresting gang  members. Known as the régimen de excepción,

09:31 it was a national state of emergency.

09:33 The changes affected almost every stage  of the legal system. Criminals no longer

09:37 had access to legal counsel and  they could be held five times

09:41 longer without charge. Options like  bail and house arrest were removed,

09:46 and police could now monitor civilian  communications without the need for a warrant.

09:50 Sentences were also massively increased.  Previously, a convicted gang lord would

09:55 get 6-9 years in prison. That shot up to 40-45.

09:59 Lower gang members saw their potential sentences  rise from 3-5 years up to 20-30. Even if you

10:05 were caught sharing gang-related information  you could end up behind bars for 15 years.

10:11 One of the ways that gangs all around the  world have avoided long prison sentences

10:15 has been by using children and teenagers for  the risky leg work. A young teenager can be

10:20 easily manipulated. What’s more, they  will get a lenient sentence and be out

10:24 sooner so they’re an expendable workforce  for the gang leaders to use as shields.

10:28 Not anymore. El Salvador lowered the age of  criminal responsibility from 16 to 12. That’s

10:35 right, actual 12-year-olds could get locked  up for decades for their roles in gangs.

10:40 Soldiers and heavily armed police swarmed the  streets, looking for any trace of evidence that

10:45 somebody was gang-affiliated. They would  raid houses indiscriminately and set up

10:50 security checkpoints on almost every major  road. Anyone passing through the checkpoint

10:54 would not only need to provide a photo ID  and proof of address but also demonstrate a

10:59 valid reason for travel. Their cars would be  searched from top to bottom. If the people

11:03 manning the checkpoints even suspected  the person could have ties to gangs,

11:07 they would ask the person to strip them and  then search their body for any gang tattoos.

11:12 This policy was massively supported up  and down the country. 78% of Salvadorans

11:18 ‘strongly support’ the crackdown. A staggering  91% of them are in favor. That’s just 9% of the

11:25 country that is neutral or anti-crackdown. The  measures were only supposed to last for 30 days,

11:30 but here we are well over two years later  and they’re still in place. That’s because

11:35 consistently every month parties across the  government of El Salvador vote to extend them.

11:40 So far, over 79,000 people have been arrested  for gang affiliation. In a country of just

11:46 6.5 million people, that’s over 1% of  their population being detained in just

11:51 two years. It’s a monumental shift and one  that has brought its own set of challenges.

11:56 The Salvadoran prison system was not  designed to house this many criminals,

12:00 nowhere close. Prisons all around the country  quickly filled to capacity. When the question

12:05 of funding came up Nayib Bukele drew a hard line  that only won him more favor. He would not take

12:11 funding away from schools, hospitals, or good  public services to feed these prisoners. Instead,

12:17 their meals went down from three to two per  day, consisting of just beans and tortillas.

12:22 But a longer-term solution was needed,  one that Bukele was already prepared for.

12:26 CECOT. A brand new 40,000-capacity prison  miles away from civilization. A proverbial

12:32 hole in the ground where they could throw  the country’s gangs and let them fester.

12:37 You know, the same hole in the ground  where you’re currently festering.

12:40 Let’s head back there and see how  your evening is going, shall we?

12:43 You don’t know what time you wake up. The  harsh lights overhead didn’t let you sleep

12:47 in the first place. The constant talking,  shouting, and fighting through the night

12:51 kept you from drifting off for more than  a few minutes at a time. At one point,

12:55 one of the tougher guys shoved you out of  the bed he wanted and you fell 8 feet onto

13:00 the concrete floor. It’s down here you  decided to spend the rest of the night,

13:04 rather than risk getting shivved for  something only marginally more comfortable.

13:08 You’re desperate to go to the bathroom, but  there’s not much you can do. One toilet in

13:12 your cell has been blocked for two  weeks now, the other got blocked

13:16 over the weekend. They’ll probably call in a  plumber… Sometime over the next year or two.

13:20 A guy shoves you in the back and you crack  your head against a bunk frame. It’s an

13:24 early lunch today. Plastic trays loaded  with cost-saving beans and tortillas,

13:29 with sickly boiled eggs on the side,  are passed through the bars one by one.

13:33 You join near the back of the line and  have to eat your cold food on the floor.

13:37 They never give out cutlery, the forks  and knives could be used as weapons,

13:41 so you have no choice but to eat with your hands  like some depressed chimp at the local zoo. A lot

13:43 of the guys in the cells have pretty poor hand  hygiene, especially with the toilet situation,

13:48 so stomach viruses are common - Which has, in  turn, made the toilet situation even worse.

13:53 You’ve avoided getting sick so far  but it’s only a matter of time.

13:57 Before you’ve even had a  chance to eat your nasty egg,

14:00 everyone is up and moving again. It’s  time for your 30 minutes. Lucky you.

14:05 Every day, you get to spend half an hour  outside. It’s easily the best part of the day,

14:09 as long as the handcuffs aren’t  done up too tight. As expected,

14:12 the guard takes a dislike to you and  pinches the shackles extra tight today;

14:17 you feel it chafe the skin of your  wrists with every movement you take.

14:20 You and your 100 cell mates shuffle meekly out  into the sweltering sun for your ‘exercise’. Some

14:26 guys try to do push-ups, some half run around  as best they can with their ankles chained,

14:31 and most just sit against the  fence breathing in the fresh air.

14:35 It’s over before you know it.

14:37 Bundled back inside by guards, the  excitement of your day is over before

14:41 it’s even 11 AM. Not that you know that.  Time’s long gone. Every day blends into

14:46 the next and the next. And most of them  are spent how you are spending your time

14:50 now. Sitting around on either a hard  bunk or hard concrete, doing nothing.

14:55 Every five days, you get your head shaved. The  four days in between usually have nothing to do,

15:00 the boredom slowly turning your brain as  soft and cold as those revolting eggs.

15:05 The fights are the only interesting part  of the day. The guards usually just let

15:08 the prisoners settle their own differences,  not worth wading into a cell with 100 angry

15:12 prisoners just to stop one criminal from getting  his face smashed in. Worst comes to worst,

15:17 they’ll flood the cell with tear gas  and send the riot squad in to drag

15:21 out the corpse. Everything else was  considered a waste of prison resources.

15:24 You think about your family. You never got to  say goodbye to any of them, it all happened

15:29 so quickly. One minute you were sitting on  your couch, the next the military police

15:32 were kicking down your door and hauling you  away. Does your mother know where her son is?

15:37 Does your daughter understand that her dad  loves her? Will she think you just abandoned

15:41 her? Will your younger brother see sense  and choose a different life? Or is he in

15:45 the next cell block over from you right  now going through the exact same thing?

15:49 While CECOT is immensely popular in El Salvador  and has indisputably helped the country get on

15:55 top of gang violence, you cannot ignore the  glaring human rights violations. So far,

16:00 not one person who has been sent to CECOT has been  released. Inmates arriving here face the very real

16:05 possibility that they will live out the rest of  their days stuck here without ever even getting

16:10 a hypothetical release date to hope for. Human  rights campaigners have accused it of being

16:14 the death penalty on a mass scale, minus the  injections, nooses, or lethal electric shocks.

16:20 With so many thousands of prisoners being  apprehended without access to proper legal

16:25 counsel, there inevitably will be a significant  proportion of innocent men behind bars. That

16:30 happens even in the best justice systems in the  world, but in one where the convicts’ rights have

16:35 been eroded to the point of almost non-existence,  it’s likely happening alarmingly often.

16:40 The lack of access to the prison is also  a massive red flag. Journalists, lawyers,

16:45 and NGOs are all either denied access or  taken around in very focused controlled

16:50 circumstances where the guards do their  best to show off the prison to the world.

16:54 The prisoners themselves have no  access to the outside world. They

16:57 are not allowed to make phone calls  or send letters like in other prisons

17:01 across the globe. They live totally  cut off from the rest of humanity.

17:05 There is a reason for this. In  countries overrun with gang warfare,

17:09 prisons can end up being pretty ineffective.  Gang leaders locked away can often still call

17:13 the shots from behind bars thanks to burner  phones that get smuggled in by visitors,

17:18 new inmates, or corrupt guards. The black market  in prison can become a hotbed of crime as drugs,

17:24 weapons, and other contraband are exchanged  freely amongst inmates. To a large extent,

17:29 gangs can continue to operate in  and through the prison system.

17:33 Not in CECOT. As extreme as the  measures are, they have snuffed

17:36 out communication among gang leaders. Lock  them away and they are dead to the world,

17:41 leaving a power vacuum in their wake. Inside  the prisons without a thriving black market,

17:46 they can’t disrupt and control things in the  way they once did. They’ve lost their power.

17:51 Some of that comes down to the way guards  are treated too. Bukele himself admits that

17:55 El Salvador had made mistakes in how they  treated their guards previously. Prisons

18:00 run by gangs saw many inmates living in  more luxury than the guards themselves,

18:04 as they’d enjoy a free flow of  drugs, prostitutes, and alcohol,

18:08 while the guards were working long shifts  in terrible conditions. Bribery was rampant.

18:13 But now, Bukele has made sure to treat  the guards much better. CECOT has great

18:18 recreational facilities for its staff.  They have gyms, lounges, and much better

18:22 working conditions. There are 1,000 guards, 600  soldiers, and 250 police officers working on

18:29 site. That works out at 40 inmates per guard,  a high ratio, but when you consider how many of

18:34 those inmates are packed into just one cell, you  can see how much more power the guards now have.

18:40 They monitor everything, they control  everything. The inmates have no power anymore.

18:46 Now check out “50 Things Nobody Tells You  About Being in Prison.” Or watch this instead!

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: $2.45 BILLION Debt. Ubisoft is DOOMED.
Video Information

• Title: $2.45 BILLION Debt. Ubisoft is DOOMED.
  • Video ID: q9GpzCudQb4
  • Published: Unknown
